pages.html:
# 6th Grade ELA — Build Standards & Conventions

This file is the master pattern. Every module in 03_Course (Canvas-Ready)/ conforms to it. Read it in full before building or reviewing any page. When a module-specific choice conflicts with this file, this file wins unless the conflict is surfaced and resolved.

Course: M/J Language Arts 1 (CPALMS #1001010) · displayed as 6th Grade ELA · course code ELA6 Audience: fully asynchronous, independent students in Canvas. The teacher only holds office hours, grades, and answers email. Nothing may require synchronous attendance, live class, or real-time peer interaction.

1. The deployment split (non-negotiable — from optima-canvas-assignments)

Content typeWhere it livesFolderCustom HTML/CSS?
Weekly lesson pages, readings, grammar mini-lessons, VR instruction pages, M365 guide & setup lessons, module-organizer instructions, course welcomeIn-lesson content (GitHub-deployed, embedded in a Canvas Page)lesson-pages/ (or _Course Shared/)Yes — full aesthetic
Module intro wrapper, module outro wrapperCanvas Quiz, survey mode, added nativelycanvas-native/No
All quizzes (auto-graded)Canvas Quizzes, added nativelycanvas-native/No
Quick Writes, VR submissions, the module project, any graded writingCanvas Assignments + native rubric, added nativelycanvas-native/No
DiscussionsCanvas Discussions, added nativelycanvas-native/No

Rule of thumb: if a teacher's eyes land on it or it scores in the gradebook, it is Canvas-native (a .md spec the teacher pastes into Canvas using only the Rich Content Editor — headings, lists, tables, bold/italic — plus a native rubric). Custom HTML is for ungraded in-lesson content only.

This corrects the old build, where Quick Writes and VR activities were custom HTML pages. Going forward, the rich instructions for a VR activity may live as an ungraded lesson-pages/ HTML page, but the graded submission is always a separate Canvas-native assignment spec in canvas-native/.

2. The four tiers & the 60/25/15 ratio

Target mix of graded items per module:

  • Tier 1 — Student & Material (~60%, 0 teacher hrs): auto-graded weekly quizzes, vocabulary checks,

completion-scored practice.

  • Tier 2 — Student & Community (~25%, light): Canvas Discussions (specific claim-and-reply prompts)

+ the outro wrapper.

  • Tier 3 — Student & Teacher (~15%, deep): one substantive teacher-graded assessment per module

— the module project. Quick Writes that build toward it may be completion-scored (Tier 1-ish) or light-rubric (Tier 2) so the module does not tip into multiple Tier-3 items.

  • Tier 4 — Ungraded scaffolding: lesson pages, intro/outro wrappers (the wrappers are also the

Tier-2 data source). Costs no teacher time to deploy.

Each module's overview.md must include a tier tally showing the module sits inside this envelope. If a module has more than one heavy teacher-graded assessment, rebalance before finishing.

3. Visual system & the lesson page form (from optima-lesson-format)

Content lessons are INTERACTIVE, full HTML documents — not RCE fragments. They are built from the optima-lesson-format interactive template (lesson-interactive-template.html), hosted via GitHub Pages, and embedded in Canvas via iframe (mechanics: canvas-interactive-widgets). This is the form that makes Optima lessons feel like Optima — and it is what fixes the branding. Every content lesson (literature, grammar, vocab, workshop) is one such document.

Palette: navy #0E1C42 · deep navy #162847 · cyan #55C8E8 · gold #C7922C · panel blue #EEF1F8 / #F4F6FA · gold panel #FDF3E3 · body text #1a2340 · muted #666.

Font: declare font-family: "Segoe UI", Roboto, Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif; on body in the interactive doc's <head>. Never use a serif font (no Georgia / Times). (Canvas-native .md specs carry no font; the RCE supplies the correct sans-serif.)

Logo: the header circle uses the real owl PNG, NOT an emoji glyph: ``html <div style="width:52px;height:52px;border-radius:50%;background:#FFFFFF;display:flex;align-items:center;justify-content:center;flex-shrink:0;"><img src="https://raw.githubusercontent.com/optimaondemand/optima-assets/eeb0b335630058906d52f478028361d352253a93/images/Optima%20Final%20Circle%20-%20Owl%20Only.png" alt="Optima Academy" style="width:50px;height:40px;object-fit:contain;" /></div> ``

Interactive lesson skeleton (match lesson-interactive-template.html exactly): <!DOCTYPE html> → <head> with Segoe-UI body rule + the full widget CSS block → <body>: .canvas-frame → navy header (owl logo, "Optima Academy Online / An Education Experience Company", "6TH GRADE ELA") → metadata strip (Quarter/Module · Lesson · Topic · Module Theme) → lavender title strip → 📖 Today's Focus (hook + intro paragraph) → 🎯 Objectives → 📋 What you need → 📚 Content cards (the teaching, with widget slots) → ➡️ What you'll do next (points to the paired Canvas-native assignment/quiz) → 💪 Wrap-up → navy footer → the widget runtime <script> before </body>. Keep the header/metadata/footer byte-stable across a course.

No preview banner. Lesson pages carry no "local preview only" / "delete before deploying" strip, and no .preview-banner CSS. Pages must look exactly as students see them at every stage, so there is nothing to remember to remove. Earlier builds of this course did include one; it was stripped from all 225 lesson pages and from the 113 live pages on 2026-08-04. Do not reintroduce it.

Widgets (the "interactive activities"): paste the widget CSS in <head> and the delegated-listener runtime <script> before </body> (both verbatim from optima-lesson-format references/widgets.md). Engines: ① reflective check-in (no wrong answer) · ② single-select rows (workhorse) · ③ scale/spectrum · ④ commit-then-reveal (<details>) · ⑤ flip card · ⑥ slider visualizer. Rotate the engine across consecutive lessons so no two feel stamped from one mold; match engine to content. Quality floor (every widget): check-in has no wrong answer; evaluative widgets give per-row instant feedback (green "why" / red nudge); vary the correct-answer index (never 0,1,2,3 in order); every widget has a Reset. Default ~1–2 widgets per lesson: a reflective check-in early, an evaluative widget after the teaching it tests. Also rotate 1–2 inline HTML/CSS visuals (timeline, labeled diagram, comparison table, ladder) where content earns one. Widgets live ONLY in these GitHub interactive lessons — never in a quiz, assignment, discussion, or wrapper (those are Canvas-native; the script won't run).

Emoji signposting — HTML numeric entities only (never raw UTF-8; raw emoji mojibakes without a charset meta). Use as section eyebrows: book 📖 📖 · clipboard 📋 📋 · target 🎯 🎯 · memo 📝 📝 · check ✅ ✅ · checkbox ☐ ☐ · chart 📊 📊 · outbox 📤 📤 · file 📁 📁 · bulb 💡 💡 · books 📚 📚 · lightning ⚡ ⚡ (widget kicker) · muscle 💪 💪 · arrow ➡️ ➡️ · headset 🧐 🥽 (VR) · warning ⚠️ ⚠️.

Canvas-native specs stay Markdown (no HTML/CSS); emoji entities are fine there too. The standalone _Course Shared guides are also full HTML documents with the Segoe-UI head + owl logo (same as lessons; widgets optional).

3c. Weekly cadence & ELA lesson rules (from optima-ela + the user's structure)

Every week, every module, follows this fixed cadence — 6 items:

#ItemFormGraded?
1–33 literature lessonsinteractive HTML lesson (lesson-pages/)ungraded (interactive checks inside)
4–52 grammar/vocab lessons, each paired with a quizinteractive HTML lesson + a Canvas-native auto-graded quiz (canvas-native/)quiz = Tier 1
61 workshop day — the week's Quick Write + the VR activity + module-project progressa workshop HTML page that points to the Canvas-native Quick Write (M365) + the VR activityQuick Write graded

So a 6-week module = 18 literature lessons + 12 grammar/vocab lessons + 12 quizzes + 6 workshop days + 6 Quick Writes + the wrappers, discussions, VR submissions, and the one module project.

The ELA 5-part structure — every literature and grammar/vocab lesson page:

  1. Topic & objectives — for this lesson only (1–2 sentences). Never preview the rest of the week.
  2. Warm-up — a short opening that meets the student where they are (use a **reflective check-in

widget**; no wrong answer). 1–3 min, ungraded.

  1. Lesson — ONE substantive paragraph of original teaching prose (not bullets). It teaches the

concept/craft/theme and drives the student into the text; it does not summarize the reading.

  1. Reading — name the day's reading on the page. For a non-PD book (all Module 1 anchor novels):

"Read Chapters X–Y in your own copy of the book." Never host or link a PDF/ebook of a non-PD book in Canvas (copyright — see Section 7). A lawful publisher/library link may be offered as [Teacher: optional lawful link]. For public-domain texts you MAY embed the text in a <details> drop-down on the page (see Section 7).

  1. Comprehension check — an evaluative widget that makes the student do something with the

reading (single-select rows, sequence, scale, flip). Ungraded; instant feedback.

Hard ELA rules:

  • Never name the method to the student. Do NOT write "hero's journey," "progymnasmata," "narratio,"

"imitatio," "disputatio," "Notice–Name–Apply," "Frye," "ekphrasis," "ethopoeia," etc. on a student-facing page (lesson OR assignment OR canvas-native spec description). assignments.title: Independent Reading Check — Q1
assignments.html:
Independent Reading · Q1 Check
Optima Academy Online · One book of your own, once a quarter
POINTS
20
LENGTH
About 3 minutes
SUBMIT
A recording
CHOOSE
Any one of four

📖 The book

Pick from The Optima Library. Three rules:

  • Not a book our class is reading this year. Check the syllabus.
  • Not a book you have used before, in any quarter or any year.
  • Something not on the menu? Ask your teacher first.

🎬 Choose how you show it

Record one of these four. They are worth the same.

OPTION 1 · ABOUT 3 MINUTES
Oral Book Response

Answer these five out loud, in order. Notes in front of you are fine; a script read word for word is not.

  1. What is the book, and how far did you get?
  2. Pick one character. What do they want, and what is in the way?
  3. Describe a moment where that character makes a choice you would not have made. Why did they make it?
  4. Read one sentence or short passage you marked, and say why that one.
  5. Who should read this book, and who should skip it?
OPTION 2 · ABOUT 3 MINUTES
Dramatic Reading
  1. Choose a passage of roughly 150 to 300 words where a character is under pressure: deciding, arguing, afraid, or hiding something.
  2. Read it aloud as that character. Decide before you record what they want in this moment, then let your pace, volume and pauses show it.
  3. Then talk for about a minute: who is this character, what do they want here, and what did you do with your voice to show it? Name one specific choice you made.
OPTION 3 · ABOUT 3 MINUTES
Make the Case

You are a guest on a books podcast and the host has given you three minutes to make one argument. House rule of the show: you have to take the side most listeners will not.

  1. Name what you are arguing about, and say where it falls in the book. Pick something people genuinely disagree over: a moral dilemma, a turn nobody saw coming, or a decision a character made that readers still argue about.
  2. Take the unpopular side and say it in your first sentence. If most readers think the character was right, argue that they were wrong. If nobody could disagree with your claim, it is not an argument yet.
  3. Give two pieces of evidence from the text: a line, a scene, something a character says or does. Say roughly where each one falls.
  4. Answer the strongest objection, the one the host would come back at you with. State it fairly first, then answer it.
  5. Land it. Finish with one sentence a listener would still be turning over after the episode ends.
OPTION 4 · ABOUT 3 MINUTES
A Different Ending

Only take this one if you finished the book. You are going to replace the ending, and you cannot rewrite an ending you never got to.

  1. Say how the book actually ends, in two or three sentences. Be accurate. The rest of this only works if your listener knows what you are changing.
  2. Name the exact point where your version branches off, then describe your ending in detail. What happens, who it happens to, and how does it finish?
  3. Explain why yours is better for this book. Not happier, and not kinder to your favourite character, but truer to what the story has been about. Name the idea or theme you are serving.
  4. Say what your ending costs. Every ending gives something up. Name what is lost by not keeping the one the author wrote.
READ IT, DO NOT LOOK IT UP
What a summary cannot do for you

All three options are built so that a plot summary will not get you through them. Here is what your teacher is actually listening for.

  • Name where you are. Give a page, a chapter, or “about two thirds through.” Summaries do not carry page numbers. Readers do.
  • Read or quote something exact. One short line, said out loud. It is the fastest way there is to show you held the book.
  • Say what you thought was wrong. Or dull, or surprising. A summary has no opinions. You do, and that is the part being assessed.
  • Stay on one moment. Retelling the whole plot is the clearest sign of a book someone did not read. One scene closely beats the whole story vaguely.
  • Be honest about how far you got. “I stopped at chapter nine because ___” earns more than a confident account of an ending you never reached.

A summary tool can tell you what happens in a book. It cannot tell you which page you stopped on, which line you read twice, or what you thought was wrong. Those are the things these options ask for.

✅ Done when

  • ☐ My book is from the menu or teacher-approved, is not a class text this year, and is one I have not used before.
  • ☐ I recorded one of the four options, all the way through.
  • ☐ I pointed at something specific in the book, not the story in general.
  • ☐ I said something that is mine: a judgement, a disagreement, or a question.
  • ☐ I listened back and I can be heard the whole way through.

assignments.html:
Written Narration 1.01 — Marcellus in the Roman World
Module 1 · St. George and the Dragon · Weekly write
POINTS
15
SUBMIT
Word document
TURN IN
OneDrive tab

📖 Reading focus

St. George and the Dragon by Michael Lotti — Chapters 1–4. Lesson focus: The Roman World — Who Is Marcellus?

📋 What you're doing

Every great story begins by showing who the hero is before the adventure finds them. In Chapters 1–4, Lotti builds Marcellus's world carefully — his rank, his duties, his loyalties, his gods. You will narrate that world from the inside, but not as Marcellus. You will write as a soldier who serves under him: someone who has watched Marcellus for months, knows his reputation, and has opinions about him. What you choose to notice, and how you describe it, reveals both your character and his.

Retelling a story in your own words is the first and most fundamental skill a writer trains: seeing events in order and rendering them in language that carries the scene. Before you can invent, you must be able to retell a story truly.

🎯 Focus question

What kind of person is Marcellus in the Roman world, and what does that world ask of him?

📝 Directions

  1. Choose one scene from Chapters 1–4 where you observe Marcellus in his Roman role — on duty, at a ceremony, giving an order, or interacting with others in his world.
  2. In Microsoft Word, write one paragraph (at least 8 sentences) retelling that scene in first person, as a soldier who serves under Marcellus. Retell events in order. Stay true to the text — you are a narrator, not an inventor.
  3. Use at least three words from the Week 1 Vocabulary list naturally. Choose words your soldier-narrator would actually use; do not force them.
  4. Save and submit your Word document following the M365 Skill Step below.

📁 M365 SKILL STEP

Before submitting, confirm:

  • ☐ Opened Word from your school Microsoft account (office.com)
  • ☐ File named: Drexel_Jordan_Narration1_ELA6 — use your last and first name
  • ☐ Title in Heading 1 style; body in Times New Roman 12 or Calibri 11
  • ☐ Saved to: OneDrive → Optima → ELA → ELA6
  • ☐ Submitted via Canvas using the Microsoft OneDrive tab

M365 Skill You're Practicing: Create, name, and format a Word document with Heading styles (Word — MOS Core)

New here? See the pinned M365 Setup & File Organization Guide in this module.

✅ Success criteria

  • ☐ My paragraph is at least 8 sentences, first person, as a Roman soldier.
  • ☐ I retell the events in the order they occurred in the scene I chose.
  • ☐ I use at least three Week 1 vocabulary words correctly and naturally.
  • ☐ My narrator stays true to the text — I invented no events outside Chapters 1–4.
  • ☐ My file is named correctly, saved to my ELA6 OneDrive folder, and submitted via the OneDrive tab.

📤 Submission

Submit your Word document (.docx) through the Microsoft OneDrive tab on this assignment. Confirm the file appears under "Submission Details." The best narrations feel like they could have been overheard on the road to Rome — so be specific.

Learning to write by copying a master's technique is one of the oldest tools in a writer's education. You study how a skilled writer does something — here, how Lotti uses contrast to set two competing loyalties side by side — and then you try it yourself. Your scene does not need to be about Marcellus. It needs to use the same technique.

Your task is to write a scene (1–2 paragraphs) in which a character is caught between two loyalties. The scene should end before the character makes their final choice — the tension is the point, not the resolution.

Your audience: Write for a reader who has not read Lotti's novel — who will encounter your scene cold, with no original to compare. The contrasting language must do its work on its own. If the reader can feel both loyalties pulling, you have succeeded; if the contrast collapses into one tone, the technique has not landed.

Why this works: for centuries, writers have learned their craft by studying how a master achieves an effect and then reproducing that technique in their own material. You are not copying Lotti; you are learning from him the way apprentices always have.

🎯 Focus question

How does Lotti use contrast — in word choice, imagery, and tone — to make two competing loyalties feel real and equally urgent?

  1. Study your model before you write. Find a passage from Chapters 5–9 where Lotti puts the dragon and the Christians side by side — literally or in Marcellus's mind. Notice how he uses different adjectives, verbs, and sensory details for each. This contrast is the technique you are imitating.
  2. Choose your character and situation. Your character need not be ancient or fictional: a young soldier choosing between orders and conscience; a student choosing between loyalty to a friend and honesty; a person choosing between family obligation and personal conviction. It must include: a clearly identified character; a complication that forces a choice between two loyalties; contrasting language for each loyalty (different adjectives, tone, or imagery); and at least three Week 2 vocabulary words used naturally. End the scene before the final choice is made.

📖 Reading focus

St. George and the Dragon by Michael Lotti — Chapters 10–14 (Dragon Fire and Christian Faith). Lesson focus: Narration in Formal Register — What Marcellus Can and Cannot Report.

📋 What you're doing

Marcellus is a Roman military officer. If he reported what he witnessed in Chapter 11 or 12 to his commanding officer, he would be constrained by that role: formal military language, only what can be observed and verified, nothing that reveals personal doubt or sympathy for the Christians.

This assignment asks you to write that report — and to think carefully about what Marcellus would leave out. The silences and omissions are as important as what is said.

Your audience: Marcellus writes to his commanding officer — a superior who expects precision, expects the formal register of military Latin, and will notice if a subordinate's report sounds like it is hiding something. The commanding officer is not a character in the novel; he is the implied reader your narration must satisfy.

Why this works: retelling has long been the foundational writing exercise precisely because formal occasions — a military dispatch, a legal account, a chronicle — force the writer to understand a subject deeply enough to report it accurately and concisely. What Marcellus includes, and what he omits, reveals what he understands.

🎯 Focus question

What does a Roman officer's military dispatch reveal about what he values — and what does his silence reveal about what he is beginning to feel?

📝 Directions

  1. Choose Chapter 11 or Chapter 12 as the basis for your dispatch. Re-read your chosen chapter before writing.

📋 What you're doing

Lotti writes Marcellus's conversion with precision and weight. The reader feels the old self receding and the new self beginning to take shape. This is craft: choosing the exact detail, the right symbol, the sentence that carries the weight of a changed life.

Your task is to imitate that craft. Write a scene (1–2 paragraphs) in which a character receives a new name or takes on a new identity. The transformation must feel earned — not announced, but shown.

Your audience: Write for a reader who has never encountered a transformation scene before — who has no way of knowing whether the moment works unless your language makes them feel it. You cannot rely on the reader knowing what baptism means or what a changed name costs. The prose must do that work.

Why this works: writers have always learned by studying a master at the level of technique, then reproducing it in their own material — absorbing the move first, then varying it. Your model is Lotti's conversion passage; your Writer's Note is the moment you name what you absorbed.

🎯 Focus question

What does it feel like — from the inside — when an old self ends and a new self begins?

📝 Directions

Before you write, reread the passage you copied in Activity 3: the moment George receives his new name or enters the baptismal water. Notice Lotti's sentence length, imagery, and use of before-and-after. Then write your own transformation scene in Microsoft Word, including all three elements:

  1. The old identity — Show who the character is before the change. What do they carry from their old life — a name, a rank, a belief, a habit? Establish what is being left behind.
  2. The moment of change — Name the precise action, gesture, word, or symbol that marks the crossing. Something must happen. Use at least one metaphor and at least one subordinate clause (beginning with because, although, when, so that, or unless).
  3. A glimpse of the new identity — Show the character on the other side. A glimpse is enough: one image, one sentence, one moment that lets the reader sense who they are becoming.

Vocabulary requirement: Use at least four Week 4 vocabulary words naturally — choose the ones that genuinely fit your character's moment; do not force them.

Writer's Note (required): After your scene, write 2–3 sentences identifying (1) the specific Lotti technique you imitated most deliberately — water or light symbolism? sentence rhythm? a subordinate clause at the moment of decision? — and (2) where in your scene you used it.

Written Narration 1.05 — The Dragon's Point of View
Module 1 · St. George and the Dragon · Weekly write
POINTS

📖 Reading focus

St. George and the Dragon by Michael Lotti — Chapters 20–21 (The Battle and the Dragon Slain). Writing focus: Narration — Point-of-View Shift, Participial Phrases, Heroic Vocabulary. Story stage: The Supreme Ordeal — the decisive battle and the hero's triumph.

📋 What you're doing

Lotti tells the battle from George's side. You know what George sees, hears, and feels. But the dragon was there too.

Your task is to narrate the battle of Chapter 21 from the dragon's point of view — to put the reader inside the experience of the adversary in its final moments. This is a narration exercise, not an invention exercise: stay faithful to the events of the chapter. Change only the perspective from which they are told.

Your audience: Write for a reader who has already read Chapter 21 from George's side — who knows what happened — but who has never considered the dragon's experience. Make that perspective feel real without making it sympathetic in a way that undermines the moral weight of George's victory. The dragon can be proud, contemptuous, ancient, even confused. It should not be pitiable.

Why this works: writing in the voice of a named figure — telling events as that figure perceives them — is an old and demanding exercise. Entering the dragon does not mean excusing it; it means understanding it well enough to write it truly.

🎯 Focus question

What does the dragon perceive, and what does it fail to understand?

📝 Directions

Reread Chapter 21 before you write. Know the sequence: what happens first, what happens next, and what the killing blow is. Then, in Microsoft Word, write your narration from the dragon's perspective, faithful to that sequence and addressing all four of the following:

  1. What the dragon sees and hears — The physical detail of the battle from inside the creature's experience. What does a charging knight look like to the thing being charged?
  2. What the dragon thinks George is — Does it recognize him as a soldier it has seen before? Does it sense something different? Does it understand what is happening to it?
  3. What the dragon thinks of the Christians — It has held the city and been worshipped. What does it make of people who pray rather than flee?
  4. The killing blow — End with the moment the battle ends. The narration must stop at death; let the reader feel the finality.

Important constraint: Give the dragon a perspective, but do not make it sympathetic in a way that contradicts the novel's moral framework. It may be proud, ancient, contemptuous, or confused — not pitiable in a way that makes George's victory feel wrong.

Craft requirements:

  • Use at least three participial phrases — one at the beginning of a sentence, one in the middle, one at the end.
  • Use at least four Week 5 vocabulary words naturally.
  • Length: 1–2 paragraphs.

assignments.html:
📋 What you are making

Over six weeks you have built something in VR: a medieval-village retelling of St. George and the Dragon — a six-panel storyboard that carries the story's arc from Roman soldier to Christian martyr. This project seals that work into a time capsule: a single Word document that gathers what you built and what you came to understand, addressed to a future reader who will walk your village before they read the novel.

You will assemble one Word document with three parts. All three are required.

🎯 The frame

Choose a relationship at the center of your capsule: St. George and one other character (Regina, Pasikrates, Agathon, Marcellus, the dragon — your choice). Decide whose voice the capsule speaks in. The pairing can be friend or foe: Regina commemorating George may be grieved; Pasikrates may be honoring; the dragon may be defiant. That chosen perspective holds all three parts together.

📁 The three parts (assembled in one Word document)

Part A — The Storyboard Record (Heading 1: "Part A — The Time Capsule Village") Insert your panoramic image of the six-panel VR storyboard so all six panels are visible in order: Ordinary World (Wk 1) · Call to Adventure (Wk 2) · Road of Trials (Wk 3) · Transformation (Wk 4) · Supreme Ordeal (Wk 5) · Return (Wk 6). Below the image, write 2–3 sentences naming what the arc shows as a story — not a list of panels. If you cannot capture the village image, paste your six weekly storyboard descriptions instead.

Part B — The Memorial in a Character's Voice (Heading 1: "Part B — A Voice from the Village") Paste a link to (or embed) your voice recording — your chosen character speaking in memory of the other. Below it, write a short caption: which character speaks, to whom, and the one thing you most wanted the listener to understand. 🥽 Note: Optima's VR platform is being upgraded — your teacher will confirm how to make and save the recording in the current app. If VR is unavailable, record the same memorial with any voice recorder and link the audio file, or include the speech as written text.

Part C — The Time Capsule Letter & Reflection (Heading 1: "Part C — A Letter for Those Who Come After") This is the heart of the capsule: a letter of 4–5 paragraphs, in your chosen character's voice, written to a future student. It is also your culminating reflection on the whole novel. Begin "Dear Future Student," and close with your name. Your letter must:

  1. Name the relationship and the arc — who you are, your relationship to the other character, and the

main interactions that changed each of you.

  1. Take a position on the character you commemorate — honor or infamy? What motivates them, and are

those motivations good? Defend it with at least three specific moments from the novel (one early, one middle, one late). (Make your case stronger: state the strongest opposing reading fairly, then answer it.)

  1. Carry a question forward — close with one genuine question the novel left you asking about courage,

virtue, identity, or what it costs to hold on to something true.

Module 3 · King Arthur · Weekly write

📖 Reading focus

King Arthur and His Knights — "Sir Gawain and the Green Knight." You now have a comparison chart (QW1); this week you turn it into a claim and an outline.

📋 What you're doing

A strong essay runs on a strong claim. Think of your claim as the engine of a car: every part of the essay that the engine does not power slows you down. Your outline is the chassis — it gives the essay strength and structure. This week you develop a working claim and plan the whole essay before you draft.

🎯 A strong claim is clear, interesting, and debatable

  • Clear — your reader can understand your main point.
  • Interesting — you and your reader care about it.
  • Debatable — it goes beyond the obvious or a summary; someone could reasonably disagree. If no one can disagree, keep refining.

You may start from this template, trying a few versions to find the one you can argue best:

"Sir ______ (name) is the ______ (positive adjective — e.g., bravest, noblest, most courteous) knight because he is ______ and ______, while Sir ______ (name) is ______ (an adjective you think Green intends as a negative contrast)."

📝 Directions

  1. In Microsoft Word, write a working claim for your two knights (try two or three versions, then pick the strongest).
  2. Build a full outline with these parts:
    • Introduction — hook, purpose, main claim, background (which parts of the story the reader needs to know).
    • Supporting argument 1, 2, 3 — one main point about your knights per body paragraph.
    • Conclusion — what your comparison shows about what makes a good knight.

assignments.title: Module Project — "What Makes a Good Knight?" Comparison Essay
assignments.html:
📋 What you are writing

A 5–6 paragraph literary comparison essay answering the module's essential question: What makes a good knight? You will compare two knights from Roger Lancelyn Green's King Arthur and His Knights of the Round Table — choose two of Lancelot, Gawain, Gareth, or Percivale — and argue what Green suggests makes a knight truly good, supported by evidence from the text.

You have already built this essay across the module: a comparison chart (QW1), a claim and outline (QW2), a first draft (QW3), stronger body paragraphs (QW4), a sharpened frame and clean quotations (QW5), and a final polish (QW6). This assignment is where you submit the finished essay for your one major grade.

🎯 Your essay must

  1. Make a claim about what Green believes makes a good knight — clear, interesting, and debatable.
  2. Compare and contrast the two knights' actions and principles, showing how each upholds or fails the ideals of a good knight.
  3. Support your analysis with textual evidence — for each knight, use at least one early, one middle, and one late moment from the book, quoted or paraphrased and then explained.
  4. Weigh the other side fairly. Name what is genuinely strong about the knight you argue is less ideal, then explain why your chosen knight better fits Green's idea of a good knight. (Answering the strongest objection is what lifts a comparison from a list into an argument.)
  5. Be organized with a clear introduction (hook, purpose, claim, background), well-developed body paragraphs, and a conclusion that says what the comparison reveals.

✍️ DRAFT WORKFLOW — you built this across the module, not the night before

📁 Draft Workflow (this is how the Quick Writes connect):

  1. Week 1 (QW1): create your comparison chart and journal in Word.
  2. Week 2 (QW2): develop your claim and outline.
  3. Week 3 (QW3): write the first full draft — name it LastName_FirstName_KnightEssay_ELA6_Draft1, saved to OneDrive → Optima → ELA → ELA6.
  4. Weeks 4–5 (QW4–QW5): revise body paragraphs, frame, and quotations — save _Draft2 (and _Draft3 if needed). Never overwrite a draft — keep every version.
  5. Week 6 (QW6): final polish, then make a clean copy named LastName_FirstName_KnightEssay_ELA6_Final.
  6. Submit the _Final Word document here via the Canvas Microsoft OneDrive tab.

🔁 Track Changes reminder: when you revise after self-review or feedback, turn on Review → Track Changes so you can see what you changed and why. Revising visibly is part of the work.

🕘 Version History note: Word in OneDrive saves a Version History automatically (File → Info → Version History). If a draft is lost or a change goes wrong, you can restore an earlier version — so save often and keep building in the same file.

📁 M365 SKILL STEP

Before submitting your final essay, confirm:

  • ☐ One Word document — your finished 5–6 paragraph comparison essay
  • ☐ File named LastName_FirstName_KnightEssay_ELA6_Final — use your last and first name
  • ☐ Saved to OneDrive → Optima → ELA → ELA6

📖 Reading focus

"Do Not Go Gentle into That Good Night" by Dylan Thomas. The villanelle's repeating refrains feel like someone refusing to give up — the form itself carries the argument.

📋 What you're doing

This week you borrow Thomas's form and fill it with your own urgent message. You will write a short three-stanza villanelle imitation addressed to someone you want to keep going — then reflect on what the form taught you. The structure is Thomas's; the content is entirely yours.

🎯 Focus question

What would you say to someone who was giving up?

📝 Directions

  1. Decide who you are addressing — a real or imagined person, an idea, or yourself. You do not have to name them in the poem.
  2. Write your two refrain lines first: a Line-1 command or plea in an urgent tone, and a Line-3 image of what you are resisting. Try to make them rhyme.
  3. Write three tercets (3-line stanzas) with an ABA rhyme pattern. End stanza 1 with your Line-1 refrain; end stanza 2 with your Line-3 refrain. (You do not have to write the full 19-line villanelle — hitting the refrains and the three-stanza structure is enough.)
  4. Below the poem, write 2–3 sentences of reflection: What was hardest about the form? What did being forced to repeat the refrain make you notice?
  5. Save and submit your Word document (poem + reflection in one file).

All three module texts — Nash, Thomas, Hawthorne. Choose one author's claim to challenge.

📋 What you're doing

This Quick Write is the opening of your project letter. You will write the first part of "Dear Author, I Disagree": you name the author's claim fairly, then state your disagreement and your own counter-claim with one piece of textual evidence. What is the most honest and specific way to say, "I think you got this wrong"?

  1. Choose the author and claim you will challenge:

📖 Reading focus

Your own "Dear Author, I Disagree" draft. Good writing happens in revision, not in one pass.

📋 What you're doing

This is a targeted revision. You will find the weakest passage in your current letter draft — where your argument is thinnest or your evidence is least clear — and rewrite it so it is noticeably stronger. You submit the original and the revision side by side so your teacher can see exactly what changed.

🎯 Focus question

What does a stronger argument look like — and can you write it?

📝 Directions

  1. Open your project draft and read it all the way through.
  2. Find the passage where your refutation is weakest — where you state a point but do not support it well, or where the author's claim feels stronger than your answer. Trust your instinct.
  3. Copy that passage into your Quick Write file and label it "Original."
  4. Below it, write your revised version, labeled "Revision." Your revision must include all three of these:
    • At least one piece of textual evidence that is new or clearly improved.
    • At least one transition word that signals the relationship between your claim and your evidence (however, therefore, because, although, as a result).
    • At least one signal verb introducing a quote or paraphrase (Nash argues, Thomas insists, Hawthorne suggests, the narrator observes).
  5. End with one sentence beginning: "The most important change I made was…" — be specific; do not write "I made it better."
  6. Save and submit your Word document.

Reading Journal Check)

M365 Skill You're Practicing: Applying Heading styles to organize a Word document (Word — MOS Core)

Build these four sections (Heading 1 each):

  1. The Big Question — copy this in and leave room to answer it as the module goes:

"When an author tells you what to believe, how do you decide whether they are right?" Write your first answer in 2–3 sentences today; you will revise it at the end.

  1. My Word Bank — a running list. Each week, add the new words you met in the reading and a short

definition in your own words. (You will pull from here when you write.)

  1. Week-by-Week Notes — a Heading 2 for each week (Week 1 … Week 4). Under each week, keep what you

noticed in the text, your close-reading observations, and anything you might use in your writing. This is where your weekly journal entries go. A good entry for this module also names, in one line, what the author seems to be arguing in that week's text.

  1. My Building Claim — one place where your argument grows. Start a sentence like *"So far, the author

I most want to disagree with is… because…"* and revise it as the texts change your mind. This is the seed of your "Dear Author, I Disagree" letter.

  • ☐ The file is named correctly and saved to your ELA6 OneDrive folder.
  • ☐ All four sections exist, each under a Heading 1.
