assignments.title: Module Project — "Dear Author, I Disagree"
assignments.html:
📋 What you are making

Across this module you read three texts that each make a claim about how to live. For this project you choose one of them and write a letter to its author in which you respectfully but firmly disagree. The move you are making has two steps: first state the author's claim at its strongest and most fair; then answer it with your own reasoning and evidence from the text. You are not summarizing the story; you are arguing with it.

🎯 Your task

Write a letter of 5–7 paragraphs addressed directly to one author — Ogden Nash, Dylan Thomas, or Nathaniel Hawthorne. Choose the claim you most want to challenge:

  • Nash — "True heroes are known by their actions, not by their bragging."
  • Thomas — "A good life is one where you fight to the end, refusing to accept weakness, decline, or death."
  • Hawthorne — "Happiness comes from having less, not more — true joy lies in simplicity and love, not riches."

📝 Your letter must do all of the following

  1. Open by naming the author's claim fairly. State their position at its strongest — the version the author would actually recognize. Do not exaggerate or distort it to make it easier to knock down. Stating the opposing view honestly is what gives your disagreement its force.
  2. Name who the author was writing for. In one sentence, say who you think the intended audience was, and point to something in the text that shows it — the words chosen, what the author assumes the reader already knows, what the author bothers to explain. A writer aiming at children and a writer aiming at adults make different choices, and knowing the target tells you why the piece sounds the way it does.
  3. State your counter-claim — what you believe instead, and why.
  4. Refute the claim with at least three specific moments from the text — one early, one middle, one late. Quote or paraphrase accurately, and credit the author.
  5. Answer the strongest objection. Somewhere in the letter, name the best reply the author could make to you, and answer it. (This is the move that lifts a good letter to a strong one.)
  6. Close by naming what you think the text is really teaching — the truth you think it gets closer to, or misses.

Argue cleanly. Your letter is itself an argument, so the standards you applied to the dragon in Module 1 now apply to you. Three moves to keep out of your own writing: do not answer the author's claim by attacking the author; do not treat a claim as proven because a lot of people believe it, or because someone famous said it; and do not restate the author's position in a weakened form so it is easier to knock down. If your refutation only works against a version of the claim the author would not recognize, it does not work.

Language requirements: at least one quotation introduced correctly (signal phrase + comma + quotation marks) and one accurate paraphrase; at least two transition words that signal the relationship between your claim and your evidence (e.g., however, therefore, although, as a result); at least one complex sentence; respectful tone throughout.

✍️ DRAFT WORKFLOW — build this across Weeks 3–4, not the night before

📁 Draft Workflow (do this in order):

  1. Week 3: create your project file in Word and name it

LastName_FirstName_DearAuthor_ELA6_Draft1. Save it to OneDrive → Optima → ELA → ELA6. Write your opening (Quick Write 3) directly into this file.

  1. Week 4: keep building in the same Draft1 file — add your three textual moments and your

answer to the strongest objection. Do your Quick Write 4 targeted revision on the weakest passage.

  1. Before submitting: make a clean copy named LastName_FirstName_DearAuthor_ELA6_Final.

Never overwrite a draft — keep every version.

  1. Submit the _Final Word document via the Canvas Microsoft OneDrive tab.

🔁 Track Changes reminder: when you revise after self-review or feedback, turn on Review → Track Changes so you can see what you changed and why. Revising visibly is part of the work, not a sign you got it wrong.

🕘 Version History note: Word in OneDrive saves a Version History automatically (File → Info → Version History). If a draft is lost or a change goes wrong, you can restore an earlier version — so save often and keep building in the same file.

📁 M365 REMINDER

Name your final file LastName_FirstName_DearAuthor_ELA6_Final, save to OneDrive → Optima → ELA → ELA6, body in Times New Roman 12 or Calibri 11 with a Heading 1 title, and submit via the Canvas Microsoft OneDrive tab.

M365 Skill You're Practicing: Draft, revise with Track Changes, and manage versions of a formatted Word document (Word — MOS Core). New here? See the pinned M365 Setup & File Organization Guide.

✅ Success criteria

  • ☐ My letter is addressed to one author and is 5–7 paragraphs.
  • ☐ I state the author's claim fairly before I answer it.
  • ☐ I name who the author was writing for and point to something in the text that shows it.
  • ☐ My counter-claim is clear, and I refute the claim with at least three specific textual moments (early/middle/late).
  • ☐ I name and answer the strongest objection to my view.
  • ☐ My own argument is clean: I answer the claim rather than attacking the author, and I have not weakened the author's position to make it easier to beat.
  • ☐ I close by naming what I think the text is really teaching.
  • ☐ I meet the language requirements: a correctly introduced quotation, an accurate paraphrase, two transition words, and at least one complex sentence.
  • ☐ My file is named correctly, saved to ELA6, and submitted via the OneDrive tab.

📤 Submission

Submit your assembled _Final Word document (.docx) through the Microsoft OneDrive tab on this assignment. Confirm the file appears under "Submission Details."

quizzes.title: Module 1 Intro — Before We Begin
quizzes.description:
📋 Before we begin

Welcome to Module 1: St. George and the Dragon. Before you begin this module, answer the questions below. There are no right or wrong answers yet — your teacher will use your responses to understand where the class is starting and to support you as the module unfolds.

This is a short reflection survey. Answer honestly; your responses are not graded for correctness.

Reading access & copyright. Students must obtain lawful access to the assigned literary work separately. Optima course materials are original instructional materials designed to support analysis, discussion, and assessment of the work. Copyrighted text, images, illustrations, panels, audio, or other protected materials are not reproduced in Canvas, VR, videos, downloadable files, or teacher resources except where expressly licensed, in the public domain, or approved as a limited fair-use excerpt for instructional analysis.

You will read St. George and the Dragon from your own copy of the book.

questions.text:
Here is the essential question for this module:

"What does it cost to hold on to something you believe is true?"

Write 2–4 sentences giving your first, honest answer. You will return to this question at the end of the module. Do not research an answer — just write what you think right now.

This module covers six weeks of reading, writing, and VR work on Michael Lotti's novel St. George and the Dragon. Many stories follow a familiar pattern — an ordinary world, a call to change, trials, a great test, and a return. How familiar are you with reading a story by tracing its stages this way?

answers.text: Very — I have traced a story's stages before to analyze it.
A little — I have noticed story patterns but not studied them.
Not at all — this way of reading is new to me.
Somewhat — I have studied it but I am not sure I remember the stages.

questions.text: How confident are you right now about reading a historical novel set in the Roman Empire?

answers.text: Very confident — I enjoy history and historical fiction.
Somewhat confident — I can handle it but it is not my favorite.
A little nervous — historical settings are new or challenging for me.
Not confident — I find it hard to follow unfamiliar historical contexts.

questions.text: Name one thing you are curious about before starting this module. It can be about Roman history, the story of Saint George, what the novel might be like, or anything else connected to this module.

This module includes an optional group-work track for the module project. Would you like to opt in to the group-work track? (Your teacher will follow up with details if you say yes. Choosing no does not affect your grade in any way.)

answers.text: Yes, I am interested in the group-work option.
No, I prefer to complete the project independently.
I am not sure yet — I would like to learn more before deciding.

quizzes.title: Week 1 Grammar Quiz — Nouns & Precise Adjectives

questions.text: Which word in this sentence is a noun? "The young tribune charged the startled bandits."
questions.feedback_correct: A noun names a person, place, thing, or idea — tribune names a person.
questions.feedback_incorrect: "Young" and "startled" describe; "charged" is an action. Which word names someone?

questions.text: An adjective answers which kinds of questions about a noun?

answers.text: Which one? What kind? How many?

questions.feedback_correct: Right — adjectives describe nouns: which, what kind, how many.

questions.text: Which adjective is the most precise for this noun? "the ______ armband" (Regina's silver dragon gift)
questions.feedback_correct: "Exquisite" — beautiful and finely made — is exactly how the book describes the armband; the others could fit almost anything.
questions.feedback_incorrect: "Big," "bad," and "nice" could describe almost anything. Which word makes a sharp, specific picture of a finely crafted object?

questions.text: In "Demetrios kept a sparse tent," the word sparse is —
questions.feedback_correct: It describes the noun tent — that's an adjective.

questions.text: A writer wants the strongest sentence. Which choice replaces a vague adjective with a precise one?
questions.feedback_correct: "Battle-scarred" shows a specific history; the others just swap one vague word for another.

quizzes.title: Week 1 Vocabulary Quiz — Words of the Roman World

questions.text: In the army of the Empire, Marcellus holds the rank of tribune. A tribune is —

answers.text: a high-ranking officer who commands a body of soldiers

questions.feedback_correct: Right — a tribune is a high-ranking officer; Marcellus commands more than a hundred men.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Marcellus is not a common soldier or a place. A tribune leads a body of soldiers.

questions.text: On the road home, Marcellus is attacked by a camp of roaming robbers. The book calls them —
questions.feedback_correct: Yes — bandits are roaming robbers who attack travelers.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Tribunes and merchants are not robbers. Which word names the armed thieves on the road?

questions.text: Marcellus's father, Titus, tolerates the Christian slaves "for order and stability." The book calls him prudent, which means —

answers.text: careful and sensible, showing good judgment

questions.feedback_correct: Right — prudent means careful and sensible in one's judgment.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Prudent is a compliment about good judgment, not about cruelty, wealth, or laziness.

questions.text: Regina's gift to Marcellus is a finely made silver dragon armband. The book calls it exquisite, which means —
questions.feedback_correct: Yes — exquisite means extremely beautiful and finely crafted.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Both Marcellus and his father admire the armband — exquisite is high praise for its beauty and craft.

questions.text: Which sentence uses raucous correctly?

answers.text: "The raucous read Cicero quietly each morning."
"He wore a raucous over his armor into battle."
"As the guests drank more wine, the feast grew loud and raucous."
"The raucous ruled the empire from Rome."

questions.feedback_correct: Right — raucous means loud, rough, and disorderly, like Lucius's drunken feast.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Raucous is not a person, a garment, or a ruler — it describes a loud, rowdy scene.

quizzes.title: Week 2 Quiz — Verb Tenses and Weighing a Reason

questions.text: Which sentence is in the simple present tense?
questions.feedback_correct: "Has" + a past form is present perfect — a past action still pressing on the present.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Look at the helper word "has." Which tense uses has/have plus a past form?
questions.feedback_general: Look for the verb with no helper word that describes something happening now.

questions.text: You want a reader to feel that a past event still matters now. Which tense should you choose?
questions.feedback_correct: "Sees" — happening now, no helper word. That's simple present.
questions.feedback_general: Simple past just reports a finished action. Which tense keeps the past "alive" now?

questions.text: Rewrite in simple past: "The Christians pray quietly."
questions.feedback_correct: Present perfect reaches from the past into the present — the action still has a grip.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Simple past just reports a finished action. Which tense keeps the past "alive" now?
questions.feedback_general: Simple past is one word, with no helper like has, have, or will.

questions.text: In Chapter 4, Marcellus overhears someone at the villa say, "If the dragon says so, it is probably right." What is wrong with that as a reason?

answers.text: It is written in the wrong verb tense
It describes something that happened before the story began
It is only one person's opinion, and an opinion is never worth listening to
It treats the dragon's say-so as proof, and saying a thing does not make it true

questions.feedback_correct: "Prayed" is the simple past — a finished action, no helper word.
questions.feedback_general: Ask what would have to be true for the sentence to work. Does a powerful creature saying something make it true? Notice that the problem is not the speaker's grammar, and not that it is an opinion. Opinions can be well supported. This one is not supported at all.

questions.text: In Chapter 6, the dragon wraps its tail around Marcellus and speaks his name, and his horse Kopto's name, in a calm, knowing voice before it makes its request. Why is knowing those names not a reason to do what the dragon asks?

answers.text: The dragon probably learned the names from Regina
Knowing a name shows the dragon has been watching him, not that its request is right
Kopto is not important enough to the story for this to matter
The dragon should have made its request before mentioning the names

questions.feedback_correct: Present perfect = has/have + past participle: "has...encountered."
questions.feedback_incorrect: Present perfect needs the helper "has/have" plus the past form "encountered."
questions.feedback_general: There are two different questions here: how the dragon knows the names, and whether knowing them makes its request reasonable. Only the second one is about reasons.

quizzes.title: Week 2 Vocabulary Quiz — Words of the Encounter

questions.text: A martyr is best defined as —

answers.text: a person who dies rather than deny a belief

questions.feedback_correct: Right — martyr comes from a Greek word meaning "witness"; a martyr dies rather than deny what they believe. Agathon is ready to be one.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Think about Agathon, who says he does not fear dying for his faith.

questions.text: The dragon asks Marcellus to bring a few sheep as a sacrifice. A sacrifice is —

answers.text: an offering, often an animal, given to a god or powerful being

questions.feedback_correct: Sacrifice — an offering of something valuable, here living animals, to the dragon.
questions.feedback_incorrect: The dragon wants to be fed. What does it ask Marcellus to give it?

questions.text: Galerius and Diocletian's harsh, unjust treatment of Christians for their faith is called —
questions.feedback_correct: To treat people harshly and unjustly for their beliefs is persecution.
questions.feedback_incorrect: The Christians are in danger from the emperor for their faith — what is that called?

questions.text: Marcellus finds one soft, scaleless spot under the dragon's wing where it can be hurt. That spot is vulnerable, which means —

answers.text: open to being harmed or attacked

questions.feedback_correct: Vulnerable means open to harm — the dragon's one weak point.
questions.feedback_incorrect: The rest of the dragon is armored in scales; this one spot is the opposite.

questions.text: "The dragon's sinewy body uncoiled from the cave." The word sinewy most nearly means —

answers.text: lean and strong, with tough, cord-like muscle

questions.feedback_correct: Sinewy describes the dragon's lean, muscular, cord-like body.
questions.feedback_incorrect: The dragon is a powerful, muscular beast — not soft, weak, or small.

quizzes.title: Week 3 Grammar Quiz — Prepositional Phrases

questions.text: Which group of words is a prepositional phrase? "The dragon leaped into the courtyard at nightfall."
questions.feedback_correct: "Into the courtyard" begins with the preposition "into" and ends with the noun "courtyard."
questions.feedback_incorrect: A prepositional phrase starts with a small connecting word (on, at, through) and ends with a noun.

questions.text: The phrase at nightfall answers which question?
questions.feedback_correct: "At nightfall" tells you when — it points to a time.

questions.text: In "The Christians prayed with quiet courage," the phrase tells you —
questions.feedback_correct: "With quiet courage" describes the manner — it answers how.

questions.text: Which word begins a prepositional phrase (a preposition)?
questions.feedback_correct: "Through" is a preposition — it can start a phrase like "through the smoke."
questions.feedback_incorrect: A preposition is a small connecting word like in, on, at, through, toward, despite. Which choice fits that?

questions.text: Which sentence uses a prepositional phrase to tell where?

answers.text: The fire spread from the dragon's mouth.
They held firm despite the heat.

questions.feedback_correct: "From the dragon's mouth" points to a place/direction — it answers where the fire came from.

quizzes.title: Week 3 Vocabulary Quiz — Words of Conflict & Endurance

questions.text: After the dragon strikes down his father, Marcellus is filled with vengeance. Vengeance is —

answers.text: the desire to harm someone in return for a wrong

questions.feedback_correct: Vengeance is the desire to repay a wrong with harm — Marcellus rides out to attack the dragon.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Marcellus is not calm or forgiving here — he wants to make the dragon pay. What is that called?

questions.text: Regina promises to intercede with the dragon for Marcellus. To intercede is to —

answers.text: plead with someone on another person's behalf

questions.feedback_correct: To intercede is to plead on someone else's behalf — Regina begs the dragon for Marcellus.

questions.text: Which word names a strong, very unpleasant smell, like the dragon's?
questions.feedback_correct: A stench is a strong, foul smell — the dragon reeks of it.
questions.feedback_incorrect: One of these words is specifically about a bad smell. Which one?

questions.text: "Weighed down by grief, Marcellus felt lethargic." Lethargic most nearly means —
questions.feedback_correct: Lethargic means sluggish and drained — the dragon's influence saps Marcellus's energy.

questions.text: After the attack, the courtyard was littered with debris. Debris is —

answers.text: scattered broken pieces left after destruction

questions.feedback_correct: Debris is the broken wreckage left behind — roof tiles and rubble after the dragon's attack.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Think about what is left lying around after buildings are smashed. That is debris.

quizzes.title: Week 4 Grammar Quiz — Subordinate Clauses

questions.text: A subordinate clause is a group of words that —

answers.text: is always a complete sentence on its own
has a subject and a verb but cannot stand alone
must come at the end of a sentence

questions.feedback_correct: Right — it has a subject and verb but depends on a main clause.
questions.feedback_incorrect: A subordinate clause has a subject and verb, but it leaves the thought unfinished — it cannot stand alone.

questions.text: In "Because he finally believed, Marcellus knelt at the water," the word because shows —
questions.feedback_correct: Yes — "because" answers why, so it shows cause.
questions.feedback_incorrect: "Because" answers the question why? Which relationship is that?

questions.text: Which word would start a clause showing concession (an idea that pushes against the main point)?
questions.feedback_correct: Right — "although" admits something that works against the main idea.
questions.feedback_incorrect: "When" is time, "because" is cause, "so that" is purpose. Which one means "even though"?

questions.text: Which sentence is punctuated correctly?

answers.text: "He converted because, the Christians showed him the truth."
"When the priest spoke his new name, the crowd fell silent."
"Although it cost him everything Marcellus changed."
"If he denied his faith. He could keep his rank."

questions.feedback_correct: Yes — the subordinate clause comes first, so it takes a comma after it.
questions.feedback_incorrect: When a subordinate clause comes first, put one comma after it — not inside it, and don't break the sentence with a period.

questions.text: Which group of words is a subordinate clause (not a complete sentence)?
questions.feedback_correct: Right — it sounds unfinished; it needs a main clause to complete the thought.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Say each one aloud. Three of them sound complete. Which one leaves you waiting for more?

quizzes.title: Week 4 Vocabulary Quiz — Words of Conversion

questions.text: At the fountain, Agathon performs Marcellus's baptism. A baptism is —

answers.text: a written agreement between two armies
a Christian rite of initiation by water, marking new life

questions.feedback_correct: Right — baptism is the rite by water; here it gives Marcellus the new name George.
questions.feedback_incorrect: The word names the rite by water through which Marcellus enters his new life.

questions.text: Pasikrates stands with Marcellus at the fountain as his sponsor. A sponsor is —

answers.text: a person who supports and stands with another at baptism

questions.feedback_correct: Yes — a sponsor supports the one being baptized; Marcellus chose Pasikrates.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Look for the word that names the supporter at a baptism — not a weapon, an enemy, or a document.

questions.text: Before the water, Marcellus makes his confession. Here, confession means —

answers.text: a statement admitting one's sins or wrongdoing

questions.feedback_correct: Right — a confession is admitting one's sins; Marcellus names the wrongs of his old life.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Just before baptism, Marcellus names his sins aloud. What is that called?

questions.text: Which sentence uses anoint correctly?

answers.text: "The army marched to anoint the eastern frontier."
"She felt deep anoint for the harm she had done."
"The anoint shone over the fountain at dawn."
"Agathon used oil to anoint George's forehead, hands, and feet."

questions.feedback_correct: Yes — to anoint is to mark someone with oil as a sacred sign, as Agathon does to George.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Anoint is a verb meaning to mark with oil — not a place, a feeling, or a light. Which sentence fits?

questions.text: To repent is to —

answers.text: feel sorrow for wrongdoing and turn away from it

questions.feedback_correct: Right — to repent is to feel sorrow for one's wrongs and turn from them.
questions.feedback_incorrect: The word is about turning from wrongdoing in sorrow — not destroying, selling, or hiding.

quizzes.title: Week 5 Grammar Quiz — Verbals: Participles, Gerunds, Infinitives

questions.text: A participle is —

answers.text: a kind of noun that names a place
a verb form used to describe a noun
a word that joins two sentences

questions.feedback_correct: Right — a participle is a verb form (like charging or wounded) used as a description.
questions.feedback_incorrect: A participle comes from a verb but works as a description of a noun.
questions.feedback_general: A participle comes from a verb but works as a description of a noun.

questions.text: Which sentence has a dangling (misplaced) participle?

answers.text: "Raising his shield, George blocked the flames."
"George, raising his shield, blocked the flames."
"Blocking the flames, George raised his shield."
"Raising his shield, the smoke stung George's eyes."

questions.feedback_correct: Yes — George is the one raising the spear, so the phrase describes George.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Who is doing the raising? That noun comes right after the comma.
questions.feedback_general: Check the noun right after the comma. Is it really doing the action in the phrase?

questions.text: In "Riding to the cave took Marcellus the better part of a morning," the bolded word is doing which job?

answers.text: describing Marcellus, so it is a participle
joining two sentences, so it is a conjunction
naming the thing the sentence is about, so it is a gerund
to plus a verb, so it is an infinitive

questions.feedback_correct: Right — as written, the smoke is raising the shield, which makes no sense. That's a dangling participle.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Check the noun right after the comma. Is it really doing the action in the phrase?
questions.feedback_general: Both gerunds and participles end in -ing, so the ending will not tell you. Ask what the word is doing. Is it describing somebody, or naming the thing you are talking about?

questions.text: Which sentence contains an infinitive?

answers.text: Agathon refused to deny his faith.
Standing at the shed door, Pasikrates listened.
The dragon's scales gleamed in the torchlight.
Arguing with the dragon was dangerous.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes — "wounded" ends in -ed and describes a noun, so it is a past participle.
questions.feedback_incorrect: A past participle usually ends in -ed or -en and describes a noun. "Charging" is a present participle.
questions.feedback_general: An infinitive is the word to plus a verb. Look for those two words together. One option opens with a participle, and another opens with a gerund.

questions.text: You want to build suspense before the main action. Where should you place the participial phrase?

answers.text: it must always go at the very end
at the beginning of the sentence

questions.feedback_correct: Right — leading with the phrase makes the reader wait for the main action, which builds suspense.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Think about "Raising his spear, George charged." The phrase comes first and makes you wait for what he does.
questions.feedback_general: Think about "Raising his spear, George charged." The phrase comes first and makes you wait for what he does.

quizzes.title: Week 5 Vocabulary Quiz — Words of Battle & Victory

questions.text: George warns his men that if they win, they will become outlaws. An outlaw is —

answers.text: a person put outside the protection of the law

questions.feedback_correct: Right — by killing the dragon and defying the Empire, George and his men become outlaws.
questions.feedback_incorrect: The word means someone who has lost the law's protection — fugitives, not generals or advisors.

questions.text: Which word names the ability to face danger without being overcome by fear?
questions.feedback_correct: Yes — Agathon prays that the men be given courage; Ionas says courage cannot come from unwilling soldiers.
questions.feedback_incorrect: "Provisions" are supplies; "underbelly" is part of a body; "bellow" is a roar. Which word names bravery?

questions.text: When the dragon rolled over, George saw its soft underbelly. The word underbelly means —

answers.text: the soft under surface of an animal's body

questions.feedback_correct: Right — the underbelly is the soft underside, the dragon's exposed weak spot.
questions.feedback_incorrect: It is part of the dragon's body — the soft underside left exposed when it rolls.

questions.text: Which sentence uses bellow correctly?

answers.text: "The bellow guided the army to victory."
"She felt deep bellow for her enemy."
"The wounded dragon let out a deafening bellow."

questions.feedback_correct: Yes — to bellow is to make a deep, loud roar, as the dragon does when struck.
questions.feedback_incorrect: A bellow is a loud roar — not something done quietly, and not a feeling or a guide. Which sentence shows that?

questions.text: After the battle, George wipes his mouth in grim satisfaction. The word grim most nearly means —

answers.text: stern and serious about something hard

questions.feedback_correct: Right — grim means stern and serious; the victory cost the lives of his men and his horse.
questions.feedback_incorrect: George has just lost friends and his horse Kopto — his satisfaction is heavy and serious, not cheerful.

quizzes.title: Week 6 Grammar Quiz — Complex Sentences

questions.text: A complex sentence is made of —

answers.text: one independent clause and at least one subordinate clause

questions.feedback_correct: Right — a complex sentence joins an independent clause with one or more subordinate clauses.
questions.feedback_incorrect: A complex sentence needs both: a part that can stand alone and a part that cannot.

questions.text: Which of these is a complex sentence?

answers.text: "George refused, and the emperor grew angry."
"Although the emperor offered mercy, George refused."

questions.feedback_correct: Yes — it joins the subordinate clause "Although the emperor offered mercy" to a complete sentence.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Look for a part that cannot stand alone (starts with although, because, when…) joined to a complete sentence.

questions.text: "When George spoke his final words ___ the crowd fell silent." What punctuation belongs in the blank?
questions.feedback_correct: Right — the subordinate clause comes first, so it takes a comma after it.
questions.feedback_incorrect: The subordinate clause leads the sentence here. A clause-first complex sentence needs a comma after it.

questions.text: Which sentence is punctuated correctly?

answers.text: "George stood firm, because he believed in the truth."
"George stood firm because, he believed in the truth."
"Because he believed in the truth George stood firm."
"George stood firm because he believed in the truth."

questions.feedback_correct: Yes — the independent clause comes first, so no comma is needed before "because."
questions.feedback_incorrect: When the complete-sentence part comes first, you usually need no comma before the subordinating word.

questions.text: Why are complex sentences useful in an essay?

answers.text: They make writing longer for no reason.
They show how ideas relate — cause, contrast, condition — instead of just listing them.
They remove the need for evidence.
They are only used in stories, never essays.

questions.feedback_correct: Right — complex sentences let you show how ideas connect, which is the grammar of an argument.
questions.feedback_incorrect: The point is not length. A complex sentence shows the relationship between ideas — "although… the book shows that…"

quizzes.title: Week 6 Vocabulary Quiz — Words of Witness & Legacy

questions.text: A martyr is a person who —

answers.text: wins a battle against an enemy
dies rather than deny what they believe
writes the laws of a city

questions.feedback_correct: Right — a martyr dies for their beliefs; the word comes from the Greek for "witness."
questions.feedback_incorrect: The word is tied to witness — a martyr testifies to a belief by dying rather than deny it.

questions.text: To recant is to —

answers.text: formally take back a statement or belief, often under pressure
write something down for the first time

questions.feedback_correct: Yes — to recant is to formally withdraw what you said you believed.
questions.feedback_incorrect: The emperor wanted George to take back his faith. That is what "recant" means.

questions.text: Which word means firm and unwavering in belief or purpose?
questions.feedback_correct: Right — steadfast means firm and unwavering.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Look for the word that describes someone who will not be moved from what they believe.

questions.text: In "His legacy outlived the empire that killed him," the word legacy means —

answers.text: the lasting impact a person's life leaves behind

questions.feedback_correct: Yes — a legacy is what a person's life leaves behind for others.
questions.feedback_incorrect: "Outlived" is the clue — a legacy is what remains after a person is gone.

questions.text: Which sentence uses testimony correctly?

answers.text: "The soldiers built a testimony in the forum."
"He drew his testimony and charged the dragon."
"George's death was his final testimony to what he believed."
"The testimony stationed troops at the gate."

questions.feedback_correct: Right — a testimony is a statement of what one believes or has witnessed.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Testimony is something you declare or witness to, not a building, a weapon, or a group of soldiers.

quizzes.title: Module 1 Outro — Looking Back
quizzes.description:
📋 Looking back

You have finished Module 1: St. George and the Dragon. Before you submit your final project, complete this short reflection. Your teacher reads every response and uses them to understand what the module accomplished — and what to carry forward.

There are no right or wrong answers. Answer honestly.

questions.text:
Here again is the module's essential question:

"What does it cost to hold on to something you believe is true?"

Write 3–5 sentences giving your answer now — after reading the novel, doing the writing, building the time capsule, and recording your VR work. How has your answer changed? What in the novel changed it?
How well do you feel you understand the novel St. George and the Dragon by the end of this module?

answers.text: 5 — I feel confident. I understand the story, its themes, and its craft well.
4 — I understand most of it. A few things are still unclear.
3 — I understand the basic plot but the themes and craft still feel fuzzy.
2 — I struggled with much of the reading and feel uncertain about the novel.

questions.text: What is one thing from this module that still feels unclear or unfinished to you — a question the novel raised that you have not resolved, a concept from the lessons that did not click, or something about the story's stages or a craft technique that you want to understand better?
Which of the seven Optima virtues did this module most require of you as a student?

answers.text: Courage— I had to take a position and defend it, even when it was uncomfortable.
Perseverance— I had to push through when the reading or the writing was hard.
Self-government— I had to manage my time and discipline my work across six weeks.
Honesty— I had to be truthful in my narrations, my essay, and my memorial.

questions.text: What single image or moment from the novel will stay with you? Name it specifically (chapter, scene, or line if you remember it) and write 2–3 sentences explaining why it is the one you will remember.

quizzes.title: Module 3 Intro — Before We Begin
quizzes.description:
📋 Before we begin

Welcome to Module 3: King Arthur and His Knights. Before you begin this module, answer the questions below. There are no right or wrong answers yet — your teacher will use your responses to understand where the class is starting and to support you as the module unfolds.

This is a short reflection survey. Answer honestly; your responses are not graded for correctness.

Reading access & copyright. Students must obtain lawful access to the assigned literary work separately. Optima course materials are original instructional materials designed to support analysis, discussion, and assessment of the work. Copyrighted text, images, illustrations, panels, audio, or other protected materials are not reproduced in Canvas, VR, videos, downloadable files, or teacher resources except where expressly licensed, in the public domain, or approved as a limited fair-use excerpt for instructional analysis.

You will read King Arthur and His Knights of the Round Table from your own copy of the book.

questions.text:
Here is the essential question for this module:

"What makes a good knight?"

Write 2–4 sentences giving your first, honest answer. You will return to this question at the end of the module. Do not research an answer — just write what you think right now.

This module covers six weeks of reading, writing, and VR work on Roger Lancelyn Green's King Arthur and His Knights of the Round Table. Which of the following best describes your experience with the legends of King Arthur?

answers.text: I know them well — I have read or watched several Arthur stories.
I know a little — I have heard of King Arthur, Excalibur, or the Round Table.
I have heard the names but do not really know the stories.
These stories are completely new to me.

questions.text: Your module project is a comparison essay — you will argue what makes a good knight by comparing two knights with evidence from the text. How confident are you right now about writing a literary comparison essay?

answers.text: Very confident — I have written comparison or argument essays before.
Somewhat confident — I can write an essay but comparing two characters is new.
A little nervous — building a claim with evidence is hard for me.
Not confident — I am unsure how to start an essay like this.

questions.text: Name one thing you are curious about before starting this module. It can be about King Arthur, knights and the code of chivalry, the Holy Grail, or anything else connected to this module.

This module includes an optional asynchronous study-partner track for the essay. Would you like to opt in? (Your teacher may pair opt-in students to swap drafts and feedback through a shared document or a Canvas message — there is no scheduled live meeting. Choosing no does not affect your grade in any way.)

answers.text: Yes, I am interested in an async study partner for feedback.
No, I prefer to complete the essay independently.
I am not sure yet — I would like to learn more before deciding.

quizzes.title: Week 1 Grammar Quiz — Nouns & Pronouns

questions.text: Which word in this sentence is a noun? "The young squire drew the shining sword."
questions.feedback_correct: A noun names a person, place, thing, or idea — squire names a person.
questions.feedback_incorrect: "Young" and "shining" describe; "drew" is an action. Which word names someone?

questions.text: A pronoun is a word that —

answers.text: takes the place of a noun

questions.feedback_correct: Right — a pronoun (he, she, it, they) stands in for a noun so you need not repeat it.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Describing is an adjective's job and action is a verb's. A pronoun replaces a noun.

questions.text: In "Arthur drew the sword, and it shone in the light," the pronoun it points back to —
questions.feedback_correct: Right — it stands for sword, the thing that shone. The noun a pronoun points to is its antecedent.
questions.feedback_incorrect: A pronoun must point to a noun already named. What is the bright thing Arthur drew?

questions.text: Which pronoun correctly matches the noun? "The knights kept their oaths, and ______ defended Logres."
questions.feedback_correct: Right — knights is plural, so the matching pronoun is they.
questions.feedback_incorrect: A pronoun must match its noun in number. How many knights are there?

questions.text: Which sentence has the clearest pronoun (no confusion about who is meant)?

answers.text: Arthur told Kay that he was king.
He told him that he was king.
Arthur told Kay that he had the sword.
Arthur told Kay that Arthur was king.

questions.feedback_correct: Right — with two men named, repeating Arthur removes all doubt about who is king.
questions.feedback_incorrect: When two people are named, "he" can point to either one. Which choice leaves no doubt?

quizzes.title: Week 1 Vocabulary Quiz — Words of Kingship

questions.text: Once Arthur draws the sword, he is named the true sovereign of Britain. A sovereign is —
questions.feedback_correct: Right — a sovereign is the supreme ruler; Arthur becomes Britain's king.
questions.feedback_incorrect: A sovereign is a person who rules, not a weapon or an object. Arthur is named the true ruler.

questions.text: Merlin hid the infant because he knew the child's destiny was to be king. Destiny means —

answers.text: the future a person seems meant to fulfill

questions.feedback_correct: Right — a destiny is the future a person seems meant for; Arthur's was to be king.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Destiny is about the future a person is meant for, not an object or an event.

questions.text: The knights of Logres were praised for their valor in battle. Valor means —
questions.feedback_correct: Right — valor is great courage, especially in danger or battle.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Valor is about bravery, not wealth, cooking, or laziness.

questions.text: The sword stood thrust into an anvil of iron. An anvil is —

answers.text: a heavy iron block a blacksmith hammers metal against

questions.feedback_correct: Right — an anvil is the heavy iron block a smith works metal on; the sword was fixed in it.
questions.feedback_incorrect: An anvil is a blacksmith's heavy iron block, not a cloth, a crown, or a lake.

questions.text: Which sentence uses chivalry correctly?

answers.text: "He sharpened his chivalry before the battle."
"The chivalry rose from the lake holding a sword."
"She wore a chivalry of white samite."
"The knights lived by the code of chivalry: honor, courage, and courtesy."

questions.feedback_correct: Right — chivalry is the code of honor, courage, and courtesy knights lived by.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Chivalry is a code of conduct, not a weapon, a person, or a piece of clothing.

quizzes.title: Week 2 Grammar Quiz — Verbs & Verb Tense

questions.text: Which word in this sentence is a verb? "Gawain quickly beheaded the green giant."
questions.feedback_correct: Right — beheaded shows the action, so it is the verb.
questions.feedback_incorrect: "Gawain" names a person, "quickly" tells how, "green" describes. Which word shows the action?

questions.text: What tense is the verb in "Gawain will return in a year and a day"?
questions.feedback_correct: Right — will return points to an action that has not happened yet, so it is future tense.
questions.feedback_incorrect: "Will return" has not happened yet. An action that is still to come is future tense.

questions.text: Which sentence keeps a steady (consistent) tense?

answers.text: Gawain rode to the chapel and waits there.
Gawain rode to the chapel and waited there.
Gawain rides to the chapel and waited there.
Gawain ride to the chapel and waits there.

questions.feedback_correct: Right — both verbs are past tense (rode, waited), so the tense stays steady.
questions.feedback_incorrect: A steady sentence keeps both verbs in the same tense. Which choice has two past-tense verbs?

questions.text: Which choice replaces a weak verb with a stronger, more exact one?

answers.text: "Gawain did a blow" → "Gawain made a blow"
"Gawain went into the hall" → "Gawain came into the hall"
"Gawain went toward the giant" → "Gawain charged the giant"
"Gawain had the axe" → "Gawain got the axe"

questions.feedback_correct: Right — charged shows bold, decisive action; the others swap one weak verb for another.
questions.feedback_incorrect: A strong verb paints the action. "Charged" shows how Gawain moved; the others stay vague.

questions.text: In "The Green Knight rides out of the hall," the verb rides is in the —
questions.feedback_correct: Right — rides shows action happening now, so it is present tense.
questions.feedback_incorrect: "Rides" describes action happening now, not already finished or still to come. That is present tense.

quizzes.title: Week 2 Vocabulary Quiz — Words of Honor

questions.text: For two days Gawain showed perfect integrity, handing over all he had received. Integrity means —

answers.text: being honest and whole in your conduct, even when unseen

questions.feedback_correct: Right — integrity is being honest and whole in conduct, doing right even when no one is watching.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Integrity is about honest conduct, not wealth, an object, or rowdiness.

questions.text: Gawain and the lord made a covenant to trade what each one won. A covenant is —

answers.text: a solemn, binding agreement or promise

questions.feedback_correct: Right — a covenant is a solemn, binding promise; the exchange bargain is their covenant.
questions.feedback_incorrect: A covenant is a binding promise, not a star, a season, or a danger.

questions.text: Riding to the Green Chapel, Gawain knew he faced deadly peril. Peril means —
questions.feedback_correct: Right — peril is serious danger; the return blow puts Gawain in real peril.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Peril means danger, not politeness, cloth, or a promise.

questions.text: Gawain's shield bears the pentangle, the Star of Logres. A pentangle is —
questions.feedback_correct: Right — a pentangle is a five-pointed star; Gawain's shield shows it as a sign of his virtues.
questions.feedback_incorrect: A pentangle is a five-pointed star, not an animal, a crown, or a person.

questions.text: Which sentence uses conceal correctly?

answers.text: "Gawain rode his conceal into the forest."
"The lord offered Gawain a fine conceal."
"They feasted on conceal at the Yule table."
"Gawain chose to conceal the green girdle from his host."

questions.feedback_correct: Right — to conceal is to hide or keep secret; Gawain conceals the girdle, his one fault.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Conceal is a verb meaning to hide. It is not a horse, an object, or food.

quizzes.title: Week 3 Grammar Quiz — Adjectives & Adverbs

questions.text: Which word in this sentence is an adverb? "Beaumains answered the steward gently."
questions.feedback_correct: "Gently" describes how he answered — that's an adverb modifying the verb.
questions.feedback_incorrect: "Beaumains" and "steward" name people; "answered" is the action. Which word tells you how the action was done?

questions.text: An adjective answers which kinds of questions about a noun?

answers.text: Which one? What kind? How many?

questions.feedback_correct: Right — adjectives describe nouns: which one, what kind, how many.
questions.feedback_incorrect: "How? When? Where?" are the questions adverbs answer. Which set describes a noun?

questions.text: In "the scornful damsel rode ahead," the word scornful is —
questions.feedback_correct: It describes the noun damsel — that's an adjective.
questions.feedback_incorrect: "Scornful" describes the damsel, a thing. A word that describes a noun is an adjective.

questions.text: A writer wants the strongest sentence about Gareth on the road. Which choice replaces a vague adverb with a precise one?
questions.feedback_correct: "Tirelessly" shows a knight who will not quit; the others just swap one vague word for another.
questions.feedback_incorrect: "Nicely," "a lot," and "quickly" stay vague. Which choice paints a sharp picture of how he fought?

questions.text: Which sentence uses an adverb to describe an action?

answers.text: "The humble youth worked in the kitchen."
"The youth served humbly for a year."

questions.feedback_correct: "Humbly" describes how he served — an adverb modifying the verb served.
questions.feedback_incorrect: In A, B, and D the describing words (humble, scornful, patient) describe nouns, so they are adjectives. Which sentence describes an action?

quizzes.title: Week 3 Vocabulary Quiz — Words of Service and Scorn

questions.text: Sir Kay is the official in charge of Arthur's household and its servants. The book calls him the steward. A steward is —

answers.text: a wandering knight with no lord
the official who manages a great household

questions.feedback_correct: Right — a steward runs the household; that authority lets Kay send the youth to the kitchen.
questions.feedback_incorrect: A steward is not a knight, a commander, or a noblewoman. Which choice names the household manager?

questions.text: The damsel speaks contemptuously to Beaumains. To speak contemptuously is to speak —

answers.text: with scorn, as if the other person is worthless

questions.feedback_correct: Yes — contemptuously means with scorn; the damsel treats Beaumains as beneath her.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Contemptuously is not kind, nervous, or wise. It describes scorn — looking down on someone.

questions.text: Beaumains chooses to serve a year in the kitchen rather than claim his noble rank. This shows his humility, which means —

answers.text: a modest view of oneself; not demanding special treatment

questions.feedback_correct: Right — humility is a modest view of oneself; Gareth refuses to lean on his rank.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Humility is the opposite of demanding special treatment. It is a modest view of oneself.

questions.text: Combat after combat, Beaumains shows great skill and bravery. The book calls this his prowess, which means —

answers.text: his great skill and bravery, especially in fighting

questions.feedback_correct: Yes — prowess is skill and courage in combat; it finally wins the damsel's respect.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Prowess is not fear, manners, or a family name. It names skill and bravery in fighting.

questions.text: Which sentence uses courtesy correctly?

answers.text: "The courtesy galloped down the road toward the castle."
"Even when the damsel mocked him, Beaumains treated her with courtesy."
"He drew his courtesy and prepared to fight."
"The courtesy of iron was thrust into the anvil."

questions.feedback_correct: Right — courtesy is polite, respectful behavior; Beaumains stays courteous despite the mockery.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Courtesy is not a person, a weapon, or an object. It names polite, respectful behavior toward others.

quizzes.title: Week 4 Grammar Quiz — Sentence Types & Conjunctions

questions.text: What kind of sentence is this? "Galahad took the seat, and the gold letters appeared."
questions.feedback_correct: Two complete clauses joined by a comma and and make a compound sentence.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Count the complete ideas. Two clauses joined by and with a comma is a compound sentence.

questions.text: What kind of sentence is this? "Because his heart was divided, Launcelot saw the Grail only in part."
questions.feedback_correct: "Because his heart was divided" cannot stand alone, so this is a complex sentence.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Can the part beginning "Because" stand alone? It cannot, so the sentence is complex.

questions.text: Which word is a coordinating conjunction (the kind that joins two equal clauses)?
questions.feedback_correct: But is coordinating — it joins two ideas that could each stand alone.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Because, although, and when make one idea depend on another (subordinating). Which word joins two equal ideas?

questions.text: Choose the best conjunction to show a contrast: "Launcelot was the greatest knight, ______ he could not achieve the Grail."
questions.feedback_correct: But signals the tension between being the greatest knight and still falling short.
questions.feedback_incorrect: So, and, and because don't show contrast. Which word marks that the two ideas pull against each other?

questions.text: Which sentence is simple (one complete clause, no conjunction joining two clauses)?

answers.text: "Galahad was pure, so he achieved the Grail."
"When the Grail appeared, the knights fell silent."
"The knights vowed to seek it, and they rode out the next day."
"The Holy Grail entered the silent hall."

questions.feedback_correct: One subject and verb, one complete idea, no joined clauses — that's a simple sentence.
questions.feedback_incorrect: A, B, and C each join two clauses. Which choice is a single complete clause?

quizzes.title: Week 4 Vocabulary Quiz — Words of the Grail Quest

questions.text: The empty seat reserved for the chosen knight is the Siege Perilous. Here, the word siege means —
questions.feedback_correct: Right — in this story siege is an old word for a seat; only the destined knight may sit in the Siege Perilous and live.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Today siege often means an army around a castle, but in this story it names a seat — the Siege Perilous.

questions.text: The Grail enters covered in white samite. A samite is —
questions.feedback_correct: Yes — samite is a rich silk; the Grail is wrapped in white samite, too bright to behold.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Samite is not a crown, a day, or a dog. It is a rich, heavy silk cloth.

questions.text: Only a knight of perfect purity can achieve the Grail. Purity means —

answers.text: freedom from sin or fault; cleanness of heart

questions.feedback_correct: Right — purity is cleanness of heart; it is the very quality the Grail tests.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Purity is not wealth, skill, or rank. It means a heart free from sin or fault.

questions.text: A hermit leads Galahad to the Siege Perilous. A hermit is —

answers.text: a holy man who lives alone in prayer

questions.feedback_correct: Yes — a hermit is a holy man who lives apart in prayer; one guides Galahad.
questions.feedback_incorrect: A hermit is not a knight, a steward, or a merchant. He is a holy man living alone in prayer.

questions.text: Which sentence uses achieve correctly?

answers.text: "The knights drew their achieve before the battle."
"She wore an achieve of white samite."
"Only Galahad was pure enough to achieve the Holy Grail."
"The achieve led him to the chapel to pray."

questions.feedback_correct: Right — to achieve the Grail is to succeed in completing the great quest, which only Galahad does.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Achieve is a verb meaning to succeed in completing a goal. It is not a weapon, a cloth, or a person.

quizzes.title: Week 5 Grammar Quiz — Paragraph Structure & Quoting Evidence

questions.text: What is the job of a topic sentence in a body paragraph?

answers.text: To list every event in the chapter
To state the one point the paragraph will prove
To give the reader a quotation

questions.feedback_correct: A topic sentence states the single point the rest of the paragraph supports.
questions.feedback_incorrect: The first sentence of a body paragraph announces what the paragraph will argue, not a list or a quote.

questions.text: Which sentence introduces and punctuates a quotation correctly?
questions.feedback_correct: Introduce the quotation with a comma, and put the closing period inside the final quotation mark.
questions.feedback_incorrect: You need a comma after "writes," and the period belongs inside the closing quotation mark.

questions.text: After your evidence, elaboration is —

answers.text: your own explanation of how the evidence proves your point
a new fact about a different character

questions.feedback_correct: Elaboration is where you explain, in your own words, how the evidence proves the point.

questions.text: What are the three parts of a strong body paragraph, in order?
questions.feedback_correct: Point (topic sentence), proof (evidence), then your explanation (elaboration).
questions.feedback_incorrect: Those are the parts of a whole essay or a debate. A single body paragraph goes point, proof, explanation.

questions.text: Which is the most common mistake when using a quotation?

answers.text: Using a comma to introduce it
Dropping it in and walking away, as if it argues for itself
Putting the period inside the quotation marks

questions.feedback_correct: A quote does not prove your point on its own; your elaboration does. Never leave a quotation unexplained.
questions.feedback_incorrect: A, B, and D are either fine or good practice. The real problem is leaving a quote unexplained.

quizzes.title: Week 5 Vocabulary Quiz — treason, mortally, brandished, barge

questions.text: Treason most nearly means —

answers.text: the crime of betraying your king or country

questions.feedback_correct: Treason is betraying your ruler or country — Mordred's crime.

questions.text: Choose the best word: "Arthur killed Mordred, but he was himself ______ wounded and could not survive."
questions.feedback_correct: A mortal wound causes death; Arthur is mortally wounded.
questions.feedback_incorrect: The sentence says the wound cannot be survived. Which word, from the Latin for "death," fits?

questions.text: Brandished most nearly means —

answers.text: waved or swung a weapon in the air

questions.feedback_correct: The hand from the lake brandished Excalibur — waved it high — three times.

questions.text: The word mortally shares a Latin root (mors, "death") with which word?
questions.feedback_correct: Mortal and mortally both come from Latin mors, "death."
questions.feedback_incorrect: Look for the word that means "able to die" or "deadly."

questions.text: Which sentence uses barge correctly?

answers.text: "Arthur was barge wounded in the last battle."
"The knight brandished his barge at the enemy."
"A black-veiled barge carried the wounded king across the water to Avalon."

questions.feedback_correct: A barge is a long, flat boat — exactly what carries Arthur to Avalon.
questions.feedback_incorrect: A confuses it with treason, B with mortally, C with brandished. A barge is a boat.

quizzes.title: Week 6 Grammar Quiz — Sentence Variety & Revising

questions.text: Sentence variety means —

answers.text: making every sentence as long as possible
mixing sentence lengths and openings on purpose
starting every sentence with the subject

questions.feedback_correct: Variety is mixing long and short sentences and varying how they open, so the writing has rhythm.

questions.text: Which is the strongest way to combine "Launcelot was the best knight. Launcelot could not achieve the Grail."?

answers.text: Launcelot was the best knight. He could not achieve the Grail. That is true.
Launcelot was the best knight and could not achieve the Grail and that is sad.
Launcelot was the best knight, but he could not achieve the Grail.
Launcelot, the best knight, the Grail, could not achieve.

questions.feedback_correct: The connecting word "but" shows the contrast and joins the two ideas smoothly.
questions.feedback_incorrect: C uses "but" to show how the two ideas relate; the others stay choppy, ramble, or scramble the word order.

questions.text: Which version varies the opening instead of starting with the subject?

answers.text: For a year, Gareth served in the kitchen.
Gareth served in the kitchen for a year.
Gareth, who is a prince, served in the kitchen for a year.
Gareth served. In the kitchen. For a year.

questions.feedback_correct: Opening with the time phrase "For a year" varies the rhythm and avoids starting with the subject again.

questions.text: After three long sentences, a writer adds: "The realm of Logres was broken." This short sentence is —

answers.text: good variety — a short sentence that lands hard on purpose
always a mistake because it is too short

questions.feedback_correct: A short sentence after several long ones lands with force. That is variety used well.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Short sentences are not errors. After long ones, a short sentence is a deliberate, effective choice.

questions.text: Revising your essay means —

answers.text: looking again at the argument to make it true and clear

questions.feedback_correct: Revision is rethinking the argument and its evidence — not just proofreading or padding.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Fixing spelling is editing, not revising. Real revision asks whether the argument holds and reads clearly.

quizzes.title: Week 6 Vocabulary Quiz — chivalry, humility, devotion, contrast

questions.text: Humility most nearly means —

answers.text: a modest view of your own importance

questions.feedback_correct: Humility is thinking modestly of yourself — Gareth's choice to serve instead of claim his rank.
questions.feedback_incorrect: From Latin humilis, "low," humility means a modest view of your own importance.

questions.text: Choose the best word: "Launcelot is the greatest knight, but his love for the queen is his fatal ______."
questions.feedback_correct: A flaw is a fault in an otherwise admirable person — Launcelot's divided heart.

questions.text: Chivalry most nearly means —

answers.text: the code of honor, courage, and courtesy knights lived by
a clear difference between two things

questions.feedback_correct: Chivalry is the knightly code — the "model of chivalry" that Logres stands for.

questions.text: To set Gawain and Gareth side by side and show their difference is to draw a —
questions.feedback_correct: A contrast is the difference between two things set side by side — the move at the heart of your essay.
questions.feedback_incorrect: The word you want names the difference you show between two knights. That is a contrast.

questions.text: Which sentence uses devotion correctly?

answers.text: "Mordred showed great devotion by betraying the king."
"The barge sailed with devotion to Avalon."
"Percivale's devotion to the Grail kept him searching past every danger."
"Gareth's devotion was a fatal weakness in his character."

questions.feedback_correct: Devotion is deep, loyal commitment — Percivale's single-minded search for the Grail.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Devotion is loyal commitment to a person or purpose. Only C uses it that way; D confuses it with flaw.

quizzes.title: Module 2 Intro — Before We Begin
quizzes.description:
📋 Before we begin

Welcome to Module 2: Poetry and Short Stories. Over four weeks you will read three texts — "The Tale of Custard the Dragon" (Ogden Nash), "Do Not Go Gentle into That Good Night" (Dylan Thomas), and "The Golden Touch" (Nathaniel Hawthorne). Each one makes a claim about how to live: about courage, about facing death, about wealth and happiness. Your job is to understand each claim — and then decide whether you agree. The module project, "Dear Author, I Disagree," asks you to write a letter to one author that fairly states their claim and then refutes it with evidence.

Before you start, answer the questions below. There are no right or wrong answers yet — your teacher uses your responses to understand where the class is starting. Answer honestly.

Reading access & copyright. Students must obtain lawful access to the assigned literary work separately. Optima course materials are original instructional materials designed to support analysis, discussion, and assessment of the work. Copyrighted text, images, illustrations, panels, audio, or other protected materials are not reproduced in Canvas, VR, videos, downloadable files, or teacher resources except where expressly licensed, in the public domain, or approved as a limited fair-use excerpt for instructional analysis.

You will read "The Tale of Custard the Dragon" (Ogden Nash) and "Do Not Go Gentle into That Good Night" (Dylan Thomas) from your own copy of each poem. "The Golden Touch" (Nathaniel Hawthorne) is in the public domain and is provided in full on its lesson page.

questions.text:
Here is the essential question for this module:

"When an author tells you what to believe, how do you decide whether they are right?"

Write 2–4 sentences giving your first, honest answer. Do not research it — just write what you think right now. You will return to this question at the end of the module.
Before this module, how comfortable do you feel writing an argument that disagrees with something you have read?

answers.text: Very comfortable — I have done this kind of writing before.
Somewhat comfortable — I have argued my opinions, just not in formal writing.
A little nervous — this feels new.
I have never done anything like this before.

questions.text:
I have read or heard of at least one of the three texts in this module before. ("The Tale of Custard the Dragon," "Do Not Go Gentle into That Good Night," or "The Golden Touch.")

  • True
  • False
Name one question you have before starting this module. It can be about the texts, the project, the assignments, or anything else.

This module includes an optional collaboration track for the project — sharing drafts with a partner through a shared document or a threaded discussion. Would you like to opt in? (Choosing no does not affect your grade. Any collaboration stays asynchronous — there is never a scheduled live meeting.)

answers.text: Yes, I am interested in the optional collaboration track.
No, I prefer to complete the project independently.
I am not sure yet — I would like to learn more before deciding.

quizzes.title: Week 1 Grammar Quiz — Common & Proper Nouns; Titles

questions.text: Which word in this sentence is a proper noun? "Belinda lived with a little gray dragon."
questions.feedback_correct: A proper noun names one specific person — Belinda — and takes a capital.
questions.feedback_incorrect: "Dragon" names a general kind of thing. Which word names one specific person?

questions.text: Which word is a common noun?
questions.feedback_correct: Right — pirate names a general kind of person, so it is a common noun.
questions.feedback_incorrect: The others are specific names. A common noun names a general kind of thing.

questions.text: Which sentence is punctuated correctly?

answers.text: I read the tale of custard the dragon last night.
I read "The Tale Of Custard The Dragon" last night.
I read "The Tale of Custard the Dragon" last night.
I read *The Tale of Custard the Dragon* last night.

questions.feedback_correct: A poem is a short work, so its title takes quotation marks, with major words capitalized and small words like of and the (inside) lowercase.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Poems are short works — quotation marks, major words capitalized, little words lowercase.

questions.text: In "Custard begged for a safe cage," which word is a noun?
questions.feedback_correct: Cage names a thing — that is a noun. Feedback (incorrect): "Begged" is an action and "safe" describes. Which word names something?
questions.feedback_incorrect: "Begged" is an action and "safe" describes. Which word names something?

questions.text: Which is the correct way to capitalize the title of this poem?

answers.text: "do not go gentle into that good night"
"Do Not Go Gentle into That Good Night"
"Do Not Go Gentle Into That Good Night"
"Do not go gentle into that good night"

questions.feedback_correct: Capitalize the important words; keep small connecting words like into lowercase (unless one starts the title).
questions.feedback_incorrect: Big words get capitals; little connecting words like into stay lowercase in the middle of a title.

quizzes.title: Week 1 Vocabulary Quiz — "The Tale of Custard the Dragon"

questions.text: What type of poem is "The Tale of Custard the Dragon"?
questions.feedback_correct: Right — a ballad is a narrative poem that tells a story, which is exactly what Nash does.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Look back at the form. The poem tells a story — that form is a ballad.

questions.text: Alliteration means —

answers.text: words that rhyme at the end of a line
a group of lines set off by a blank space
the repeating of the same beginning sound in nearby words
giving human feelings to a non-human thing

questions.feedback_correct: Correct — like the /b/ in "brave as a barrel full of bears."
questions.feedback_incorrect: Listen to the beginnings of words. Alliteration repeats the same beginning sound.

questions.text: When Custard "cried for a nice safe cage," giving a dragon human feelings is an example of —
questions.feedback_correct: Right — personification gives human feelings or actions to something that isn't human.
questions.feedback_incorrect: A dragon is not human. What do we call giving it human feelings?

questions.text: Which word means almost the same as cowardly?
questions.feedback_correct: Yes — timid and cowardly both describe shrinking from danger.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Think about what cowardly means — fearful, avoiding danger. Which word matches?

questions.text: In the poem, the little pets boast all day. To boast means to —

answers.text: talk with too much pride about yourself

questions.feedback_correct: Correct — to boast is to talk with too much pride about yourself, which the pets keep doing.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Re-read what the pets do — they keep telling everyone how great they are.

quizzes.title: Week 2 Grammar Quiz — Action & Linking Verbs; Apostrophes

questions.text: Which word is an action verb in this sentence? "The old men rage at the closing dark."
questions.feedback_correct: Rage shows something happening — that is an action verb.
questions.feedback_incorrect: "Old" describes and "men" names. Which word shows the men doing something?

questions.text: Which word is a linking verb in this sentence? "The light is faint at evening."
questions.feedback_correct: Is links the subject "light" to the describing word "faint" — a linking verb.
questions.feedback_incorrect: A linking verb connects the subject to a description. Which word does that here?

questions.text: Which sentence uses the apostrophe correctly for a contraction?
questions.feedback_correct: Don't = do not; the apostrophe replaces the missing "o."
questions.feedback_incorrect: A contraction's apostrophe goes where letters are missing — between "n" and "t" in don't.

questions.text: Which phrase correctly shows that the tears belong to the father?
questions.feedback_correct: Add 's to a singular owner: the father's tears.
questions.feedback_incorrect: For one owner, add apostrophe + s: the father's tears.

questions.text: Which sentence is correct?

answers.text: It's getting dark, and the lamp has lost its glow.
Its getting dark, and the lamp has lost it's glow.
Its' getting dark, and the lamp has lost its' glow.
It's getting dark, and the lamp has lost it's glow.

questions.feedback_correct: It's = "it is"; its (no apostrophe) shows ownership. This sentence uses both correctly.
questions.feedback_incorrect: It's always means "it is." Its (no apostrophe) means "belonging to it."

quizzes.title: Week 2 Vocabulary Quiz — "Do Not Go Gentle into That Good Night"

questions.text: What kind of poem is "Do Not Go Gentle into That Good Night"?
questions.feedback_correct: Right — a villanelle is the 19-line form built on two returning lines.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Look back at the form lesson. A 19-line poem with two repeating lines is a villanelle.

questions.text: A refrain is —

answers.text: the last word of every line
a line that repeats at set points, like a chorus

questions.feedback_correct: Correct — a refrain returns again and again, like a chorus.
questions.feedback_incorrect: A refrain is a whole line that keeps coming back, like a song's chorus.

questions.text: Figurative language means language that —

answers.text: means exactly what it says, word for word
means something other than its plain, literal sense
is always written in capital letters
only appears in stories, never in poems

questions.feedback_correct: Right — like "that good night" meaning death, not a real night.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Figurative language carries a meaning beyond the literal one — "night" standing for death.

questions.text: In the poem, to rage against the dying of the light means to —
questions.feedback_correct: Correct — rage is strong, fierce resistance, the opposite of going "gentle."
questions.feedback_incorrect: Rage names fierce, burning resistance — the opposite of accepting quietly.

questions.text: Which word means almost the same as grieve?
questions.feedback_correct: Yes — to grieve and to mourn both mean to feel deep sadness over a loss.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Grieve means deep sadness over a loss. Which word matches that?

quizzes.title: Week 3 Grammar Quiz — Adjectives & Complex Sentences

questions.text: Which word is the adjective in this sentence? "Midas counted his gold coin in the dreary dungeon."
questions.feedback_correct: Right — dreary describes the dungeon, telling what kind it is, so it is an adjective.
questions.feedback_incorrect: An adjective describes a noun. Which word tells you what the dungeon is like?

questions.text: An adjective is a word that —

answers.text: names a person, place, or thing

questions.feedback_correct: Correct — an adjective describes a noun (which one, what kind, or how many).
questions.feedback_incorrect: An adjective describes a noun, like golden in "golden statue."

questions.text: Which sentence is a complex sentence?

answers.text: Midas loved gold and counted it daily.
Because Midas loved gold, he ignored his daughter.

questions.feedback_correct: Right — it joins a main idea to a smaller one with because, so it is complex.
questions.feedback_incorrect: A complex sentence joins two ideas with a word like because or when. Which one does that?

questions.text: Which sentence is punctuated correctly?

answers.text: When the sun rose Midas touched the bed.
When, the sun rose Midas touched the bed.
When the sun rose, Midas touched the bed.
When the sun rose Midas, touched the bed.

questions.feedback_correct: Correct — when the when/because part comes first, put a comma after it.
questions.feedback_incorrect: If the connecting word starts the sentence, a comma goes after the first part.

questions.text: In "the burnished golden cup," how many adjectives describe the noun cup?
questions.feedback_correct: Right — burnished and golden both describe cup, so there are two adjectives.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Count the describing words before cup: burnished and golden.

quizzes.title: Week 3 Vocabulary Quiz — "The Golden Touch"

questions.text: In the story, the cup had a burnished surface. Burnished means —
questions.feedback_correct: Right — burnished means polished until it shines, like the gold cup and the staircase rail.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Picture the gleaming gold cup. Burnished means polished and shining.

questions.text: Which word is the closest synonym for disconsolate?
questions.feedback_correct: Correct — disconsolate and inconsolable both mean too sad to be comforted.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Disconsolate means so sad nothing comforts you. Which word matches that?

questions.text: When Midas cannot eat his golden breakfast, he thinks, "Well, this is a quandary!" A quandary is —
questions.feedback_correct: Right — a quandary is a difficult, puzzling situation with no easy way out.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Midas has a costly breakfast he cannot eat. A quandary is a difficult, puzzling fix.

questions.text: What is the turning point of "The Golden Touch"?

answers.text: Midas first locks himself in the treasure room
Midas kisses Marygold and she turns to gold
Midas turns the roses to gold

questions.feedback_correct: Right — the kiss that turns Marygold to gold is the turning point; after it, the worst has happened and nothing can go back.
questions.feedback_incorrect: The turning point is the moment everything changes and cannot be undone. Which event does that?

questions.text: You can see Midas's wish is dangerous long before Midas can. When the reader knows something a character does not, that is —
questions.feedback_correct: Correct — that is dramatic irony: the reader knows the danger the character cannot see.
questions.feedback_incorrect: When the reader knows more than the character, the term is dramatic irony.

quizzes.title: Week 4 Grammar Quiz — Transitions

questions.text: A transition word is one that —

answers.text: names a person, place, or thing
shows how one idea connects to the next

questions.feedback_correct: Right — a transition is a signpost that shows how ideas connect (adding, contrasting, or concluding).
questions.feedback_incorrect: A transition links ideas. It tells the reader what the next sentence is doing.

questions.text: You are about to turn from the author's view to your own answer. Which transition fits best?
questions.feedback_correct: Right — however signals a contrast, which is what you need when you turn to disagree.
questions.feedback_incorrect: You are pushing against the author. Which word warns the reader of a contrast?

questions.text: Which transition signals a conclusion?
questions.feedback_correct: Correct — therefore signals a conclusion, the result you draw from your reasoning.
questions.feedback_incorrect: A conclusion word draws a result. However and although show contrast; which one concludes?

questions.text: Which sentence uses an adding transition correctly?

answers.text: The roses turned to gold. However, they smelled sweet.
The roses turned to gold therefore Midas was rich.
The roses, although, turned to gold.
The roses turned to gold. In addition, the food became metal.

questions.feedback_correct: Right — in addition stacks another point of the same kind onto the first.
questions.feedback_incorrect: An adding transition piles on a similar point. Which sentence adds rather than contrasts?

questions.text: Which transition shows a contrast?
questions.feedback_correct: Correct — although signals a contrast, a qualifying or opposite idea.
questions.feedback_incorrect: A contrast word warns of an opposite idea. Furthermore and in addition add; which one contrasts?

quizzes.title: Week 4 Vocabulary Quiz — Words for Arguing Well

questions.text: To concede a point means to —
questions.feedback_correct: Right — to concede is to admit a point against you is true, which is the fair move in a strong argument.
questions.feedback_incorrect: To concede is to grant that the other side is right about something.

questions.text: Which word is the closest synonym for persuade?
questions.feedback_correct: Correct — to persuade and to convince both mean to lead someone to agree with you.
questions.feedback_incorrect: To persuade is to lead a reader to agree. Which word matches that?

questions.text: To assert a claim means to —
questions.feedback_correct: Right — to assert is to state firmly that something is true.
questions.feedback_incorrect: To assert is to state something firmly, not to question or hide it.

questions.text: A claim is a sentence that —

answers.text: only states a fact no one can argue with
takes a position a thoughtful person could disagree with
lists the events of a story

questions.feedback_correct: Right — a claim takes a position someone could disagree with; that is what makes it arguable.
questions.feedback_incorrect: A claim takes a stand. A fact ("the poem has 15 stanzas") is not a claim because no one can argue it.

questions.text: A counter-argument is —

answers.text: the strongest version of your own claim
the opposing side, the case against your claim

questions.feedback_correct: Right — a counter-argument is the opposing side; a strong letter states it fairly, then answers it.
questions.feedback_incorrect: A counter-argument is the case against your claim, the view you answer in your letter.
