discussions.title: Week 2 Discussion — Two Powers
discussions.html:
📖 This week

You read about Marcellus encountering two very different powers: the dragon and the Christians. Both are demanding something from the people around them. Both shape what life looks like in the city.

🎯 Focus

How does Lotti use contrast in Chapters 5–9 to set these two powers against each other?

📝 Your post (answer both parts — 5–8 sentences total)

  1. State one specific claim about how Lotti uses contrast in Chapters 5–9. Your claim should name something specific — a scene, a moment, a description — not just a general observation.
    • Weak claim: "Lotti uses contrast to show that the dragon and the Christians are different."
    • Stronger claim: "When Lotti describes the dragon's worshippers cowering in silence and then immediately shows the Christians singing in the hidden room, he uses contrast to show that fear and faith produce completely different communities."
  2. Write your claim, then give the specific evidence (scene or passage) that supports it.

📝 Your reply (respond to one classmate)

Do you agree with their claim? If so, strengthen it — add a piece of evidence they did not use. If not, respectfully explain where you think the contrast works differently than they described. Your reply must engage their actual argument, not just say "good point."

✅ Success criteria

  • ☐ My post makes a specific, arguable claim about contrast and names a scene or passage.
  • ☐ I support the claim with evidence from Chapters 5–9.
  • ☐ My reply engages a classmate's actual argument and adds or challenges something.
  • ☐ Both my post and reply are submitted before the week closes.

discussions.title: Week 4 Discussion — Is It Ever Right to Abandon the Identity You Were Born With?
discussions.html:
🎯 This week's debate question

Is it ever right to abandon the identity you were born with?

George gives up his Roman name, his rank, and the religion of his family. The story calls this his Transformation — the moment he becomes someone new. But some would call it a betrayal.

📝 Your post (take a side and defend it — 6–10 sentences)

State whether you think it IS or IS NOT ever right to abandon the identity you were born with. Then do three things:

  1. Give the strongest version of the opposing argument — the one your opponent would make. State it fairly enough that someone who disagreed with you would recognize it.
  2. Explain why, despite that argument, your position is better supported — using specific evidence from the novel.
  3. Add one sentence at the end. In Chapter 15, Regina wants Marcellus to do something and gives him reasons. She calls him "a dishonest, disloyal man," and she reminds him that her father has connections to Galerius. Pick one of those two and say what is wrong with it as a reason. Attacking someone's character is not the same as answering their point, and knowing powerful people is not the same as being right.

You do not have to agree with Lotti's answer. You have to defend your own answer with reasoning.

📝 Your reply (respond to one classmate who took the OPPOSITE position)

Do not just disagree. Find one part of their argument you think is genuinely strong — acknowledge it — and then explain where and why your argument is stronger.

✅ Success criteria

  • ☐ My post clearly states my position (IS / IS NOT).
  • ☐ I state the strongest opposing argument fairly, then explain why my position is better supported.
  • ☐ I use specific evidence from the novel.
  • ☐ I added one sentence naming what is wrong with one of Regina's reasons in Chapter 15.
  • ☐ My reply engages a classmate who took the opposite position, names a genuine strength, then presses my case.

discussions.title: All-Class Forum 1 — One Life Against the Estate
discussions.html:
All-Class Forum 1 — One Life Against the Estate
Module 1 · St. George and the Dragon · closes end of Week 4
POINTS
25
FORMAT
Post + two replies
SETTING
Post before you can see replies

📖 Where we are

By Chapter 15 the dragon has burned the estate once, three people are dead, and Titus lies stricken and unresponsive. Marcellus rides to Lucius's villa and is snubbed at the door. Then Regina makes her request: hand over one slave, a sick and old one, and the dragon will be satisfied. One life, and the estate is safe. He refuses, sets the dragon armband on the floor, and walks out.

🎯 The question

Regina asks for one sick, old slave. One life, and the estate is safe. Marcellus says no. Was he right?

Every position here is defensible from the book, which is what makes it worth arguing. Before you answer, notice that Marcellus is not choosing between right and wrong. He is choosing between two things he genuinely owes.

📝 Your first post

  1. Take a position and say it in your first sentence. He was right, or he was wrong. Do not build up to it.
  2. Name the two principles he is choosing between, in your own words. Say what each one would have him do. One of them says a person is not a price, whatever the arithmetic. The other says a man responsible for a whole estate has to weigh one life against many. Give each one its strongest form, even the one you are arguing against.
  3. Name who paid for his choice, and what it cost them. This is the part that stops the question being abstract. Titus, Regina, Pasikrates, the slaves who stayed, and later Petrus, Lucas and Dionysius. Pick one person and say specifically what his decision cost them.
  4. Answer the strongest objection to your own position. If you say he was right, the strongest objection is that people who trusted him died for a principle they were never asked about. If you say he was wrong, the strongest objection is that handing over a person to save property is the exact thing the dragon has wanted from him since Chapter 6.

Then add one more sentence. In this same scene Regina gives Marcellus reasons. She calls him “a dishonest, disloyal man,” and she reminds him that her father has connections to Galerius. Pick one of those two and say what is wrong with it as a reason. Attacking someone's character is not the same as answering their point, and knowing powerful people is not the same as being right.

You will not be able to see anyone else's post until you have written yours. That is on purpose. Work out what you actually think first.

💬 Your replies

Reply to at least two classmates. Look for posts that took a different position from yours, or the same position for a different reason. In each reply, do one of these three things:

  • Add. Give a second piece of evidence for their claim that they did not use.
  • Challenge. Name the part of their reasoning you think is wrong, and say why.
  • Ask. Ask them something their post left open, in a way they could actually answer.

🙋 Optional: the questions thread

There is a thread at the top called Questions about the book. Post anything you genuinely wondered about while reading. Questions there are ungraded extra contributions, and you never lose points for asking one.

💬 How we talk to each other in this forum

  • Write in complete sentences. No text-speak, no all-lowercase posts.
  • Your first post answers every part of the prompt and names a specific moment in the text: a scene, a line, a description. Not “the book shows” but “in Chapter 7, when ___.”
  • Reply to at least two classmates. A reply adds something, challenges something, or asks something. “I agree” and “good point” are not replies.
  • Stay on the question. If you want to raise something else about the book, that is what the questions thread is for.
  • Make it your own. Read what is already posted. If someone has made your point, either build on it and say something new, or take a different position. Do not restate.
  • Disagree with the idea, not the person. Name what they said, say why you see it differently, and keep it courteous. You are allowed to change your mind in public. That is a good sign, not a bad one.
  • Questions count. Post a genuine question about the text any time and it counts as an extra contribution. You do not have to know the answer to ask a good question.

✅ Done when

  • ☐ My first post takes a position in its first sentence.
  • ☐ I named both principles he was choosing between, and gave each its strongest form.
  • ☐ I named a specific person and what his choice cost them.
  • ☐ I answered the strongest objection to my own position.
  • ☐ I added the sentence about what is wrong with one of Regina's reasons.
  • ☐ I replied to two classmates, and each reply adds, challenges, or asks.

discussions.title: Week 6 Discussion — Is George's Martyrdom a Defeat or a Victory?
discussions.html:
🎯 The final debate question for this module

Is George's martyrdom a defeat or a victory?

Here are the two clearest positions:

  • Defeat: George is captured, tried, and executed by the state. His physical life ends. He does not return home. His death changes nothing immediately in the political situation of Christians in the Roman Empire.
  • Victory: George stands before the emperor's court and does not recant. He dies with his testimony intact. His memory outlasts Rome. He becomes the patron saint of nations. His death is his final and most consequential act.

There is also a third position — that these two cannot be separated, that his death is both defeat and victory at once, and that Lotti intends the reader to hold both together.

📝 Your post (6–10 sentences)

Choose one position — Defeat, Victory, or Both — and defend it. Use at least one specific scene from Chapters 22–24 as evidence. Use at least one vocabulary word from any week of this module.

📖 Where we are

A green man rides into Camelot at a feast and offers a bargain: strike me once, and in a year I strike you once. Gawain takes it. He spends the year riding north to keep an appointment he expects to be killed at.

At the castle where he shelters, he agrees to a second bargain: each day, they exchange whatever they have won. He hands over what he receives. Except once. He keeps a green girdle because he is told it will save his life, and he does not hand it over.

📖 Where we are

Dylan Thomas wrote "Do Not Go Gentle into That Good Night" for his dying father. It is not a poem about death in general. It is a son telling his father what to do, six times over, in a form so strict that the same two lines have to keep coming back.

This week you also read Shakespeare's Sonnet 18, which is fourteen lines long and turns on a single word in the middle.
